# What Happened to Eudora, the Email Client That Taught the Internet to Write

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-eudora-email-client.html
Author: Theo Lindqvist (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-09
Topics: Software & Apps, Internet Culture, Then vs Now

## In February 1996, Eudora Owned Email. By 2006, It Was Dead.

Here's a number that feels impossible in retrospect: in February 1996, Eudora had 10 million users. By December 1996, that number had grown to 18 million. In 1995, Qualcomm, the company that owned Eudora, claimed 64.7 percent of all email software revenues. The year before, 1994, the company had generated $4.2 million in revenue. By 1996, that number had jumped to $33.7 million. Eudora wasn't just popular. Eudora was the category.

This was the internet's golden moment for a specific kind of software. Not web-based. Desktop-based. A program you installed on your computer. A tool that sat on your machine and handled one job: email. And Eudora didn't just do email. It taught people how to use email properly. It had features that seemed obvious once Eudora did them, and revolutionary before that. It had a search interface that actually worked. It had organizational tools that made sense. It had filters that could process mail automatically. It had a way of displaying threads that showed you what you were replying to.

And then, slowly, it disappeared. The last Qualcomm version shipped on October 11, 2006. Version 7.1.0.9 for Windows. Version 6.2.4 for Mac. That was it. No new versions. No updates. Just discontinuation. Today, Eudora is remembered primarily by people who used it, which is to say it's almost entirely forgotten. This is the story of how the internet's first truly modern email client got replaced by webmail, and why that replacement feels inevitable in retrospect but was basically nobody's plan at the time.

## Before Eudora, Email Clients Were a Disaster

You have to understand the baseline here. Before Eudora, email on personal computers was pretty rough. Email wasn't unified. You might check email from work on a different system than you checked email at home. There was no standardization. There were a bunch of competing protocols and terrible user interfaces. The experience of checking email was genuinely unpleasant. It required technical knowledge. It required patience.

And then in 1988, a graduate student named Steve Dorner at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built Eudora. He built it for the Mac, because that's what he had access to. He built it with something like 50,000 lines of C code. And he named it after Eudora Welty, the Mississippi writer, specifically after her short story "Why I Live at the P.O." The tagline became "Bringing the P.O. to Where You Live," and if you think about it, that's actually a pretty good description of what email does.

Eudora worked. It had a clean interface. It had features that made sense once you saw them. It let you organize mail. It let you search. It let you set up filters so mail could be automatically processed and filed. These seem like obvious features now. In the early 1990s, they were not obvious. They were revelatory.

Dorner was working remotely from Illinois when Qualcomm licensed Eudora from the University of Illinois in 1991 and hired him to continue development. This is where the story gets interesting. Qualcomm is a telecom giant. They're in the business of networking, telecommunications, semiconductors. Email software seems like a weird thing for them to own. But they owned it, and they committed resources to it, and they built it into a dominant product through the 1990s.

## The Three-Tier Model: Free, Sponsored, and Pro

One of the reasons Eudora became so dominant was their business model. They offered three tiers: Eudora Light, which was free. Eudora Pro, which was paid at $49.95. And Eudora Sponsored, which was free but showed advertising. This was a smart approach. It let everyone use the product. It got students using Eudora, which meant that when those students got jobs, they wanted to use Eudora at work. It let people try before they paid. And it gave Eudora users a choice about how they wanted to engage with the product.

By the late 1990s, Eudora had installed itself into the infrastructure of email. Businesses used it. ISPs recommended it. People used it at home and at work. Eudora's dominance wasn't fragile. It was structural. The revenue kept growing. The user base kept expanding. Eudora owned the segment of standalone email clients so completely that the question of what the second-place email client was seemed almost irrelevant.

Then, in 1999, the company started offering Eudora Sponsored, an ad-supported free version. This model had worked before, but ad-supported software was becoming more culturally sensitive. People didn't necessarily love the idea of advertisements in their email client. And by 2000, Eudora Sponsored had hit 1 million active users. Which sounds good until you realize it's 1 million people who would have been paying customers and instead were ad-supported users. The math got worse every year.

The real question is this: they weren't stupid. They just didn't see what was coming. Nobody did.

## The Bundling Problem: How Microsoft Destroyed Eudora Without Really Trying

In 1997, Microsoft released Windows 95 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/the-night-windows-95-launched.html) with Outlook Express bundled in. Outlook Express was not as good as Eudora. It had fewer features. It was simpler, which was sometimes an advantage and sometimes a limitation. But it was free, and it came with Windows, and for a significant portion of computer users, having an email client pre-installed was enough. Why buy Eudora Pro when Outlook Express comes with your operating system?

This is essentially what every smartphone company did years later when they bundled email clients into iOS and Android. But in 1997, when it happened to Eudora, it was devastating. Eudora's install base started flattening. New users saw no reason to install a third-party email client when Windows came with one. Eudora's growth narrative broke. The user numbers that had been accelerating started stabilizing. The financial dynamics started shifting.

Qualcomm tried to adapt. They made Eudora more powerful, more feature-rich, more sophisticated. But sophisticated email clients are actually harder to use, and a lot of users just wanted simple email. And if they wanted simple email, why not use what came with their operating system?

## Webmail Arrived and Changed Everything

Then Hotmail (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-everyone-had-hotmail-account.html) launched in 1996. This is where the logic starts to break down, at least from Qualcomm's perspective. Hotmail introduced the concept of email that you didn't need to install anything to access. You just went to a website. You logged in. You checked your email. You didn't need a client. You didn't need software. You just needed a web browser.

For people who checked email from multiple computers, webmail was enormously appealing. Eudora required you to set up email on each machine separately. Webmail just worked from any computer. For people with laptops who checked email on the road, webmail started looking like the future. You didn't need to download messages. You didn't need to manage storage. You just accessed your email from anywhere.

Hotmail grew incredibly fast. Microsoft bought Hotmail in 1997 and integrated it into their services. More competition in webmail launched. Yahoo (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-yahoo-now.html) Mail. AOL (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/does-aol-still-exist-today.html) Mail. Webmail went from novelty to normal incredibly quickly. By the early 2000s, webmail was where email growth was happening. Desktop email clients were becoming artifacts of the previous era.

## Gmail Arrived and Finished the Job

And then, in 2004, Google launched Gmail. Gmail was webmail, but it was webmail with conversation threading, powerful search, spam filtering that actually worked, and enough free storage that nobody ever needed to delete emails. Gmail was everything Eudora had been for the standalone client market, but delivered through a web browser instead of an application.

Gmail didn't kill Eudora overnight. But Gmail represented the end of an era. The real question is this: why would you use a desktop email client anymore? Why would you install software? Why wouldn't you just use Gmail? Gmail had everything. Search that worked. Organization that made sense. Accessibility from anywhere. No installation. No storage management. Just email.

Qualcomm's last version of Eudora shipped in October 2006, two years after Gmail's launch. It took two years for the company to acknowledge that the market had fundamentally changed. By then, it was already over. Email as a category had moved entirely to the web. Eudora was a remnant. An excellent remnant, but a remnant.

## The Open Source Attempt: Too Late, Too Little

Qualcomm did try one more thing. They open-sourced Eudora as a project called Penelope, based on the Mozilla Thunderbird framework. The idea was that a community of developers could keep the software alive and relevant. But here's the thing: the market had already moved. Nobody was interested in developing or using a desktop email client anymore. The effort continued until around 2010, then was fully deprecated by 2013. The code was eventually donated to the Computer History Museum in 2018, where it sits as a historical artifact.

This is what happened to Eudora. Not a dramatic collapse. Not a technical failure. Just obsolescence. The email market shifted to webmail, and desktop clients became unnecessary. Eudora was the best desktop email client ever built. But desktop email clients stopped being relevant. The market didn't need the best desktop email client. It just needed email. And email, increasingly, existed on the web.

## Why This Matters Now

Look at what happened: a company with dominant market position, a great product, significant revenue, and technical excellence got completely displaced because the category itself changed. This wasn't about execution. Qualcomm executed well. This was about the market fundamentally shifting from desktop software to web services. And once that shift happened, no amount of product quality could change the outcome.

This is a lesson that echoes through software constantly. Dominance in a shrinking market is just a slow decline. Eudora had 18 million users and owned 64.7 percent of email software revenue. And none of that mattered once email itself moved to the web. The category got disrupted. The leader in the old category got disrupted with it.

Eudora's legacy is weird because it's simultaneously huge and invisible. Eudora established conventions that every email client since has followed. Threading. Search. Filters. Good spam handling. Conversation views. Eudora did these things first and did them right. Gmail and every other email service since has built on Eudora's design language, probably without even realizing it. So Eudora won in design but lost in business. It taught the internet how to do email. And then it vanished.

## The Transition Was Inevitable, But Not Obvious at the Time

This is the weird thing about Eudora's decline: there's no villain in this story. Qualcomm didn't make bad decisions. They made rational decisions based on available information. They controlled 64.7 percent of email software revenue. They had millions of users. Revenue was growing. And then the category itself shifted, and none of that mattered anymore. This happens in technology regularly, and it's almost always surprising to the people living through it.

The shift from desktop email to webmail wasn't obvious in 1996. Desktop email seemed like the natural evolution. You install software on your computer. It manages your email locally. You have control. You have privacy, sort of. You have your data on your machine. This seemed obviously superior to the idea of logging into a website to check email, which felt weird and fragile. It required internet connectivity every time. It meant your email was on someone else's servers.

But convenience beats theoretical concerns. Webmail was convenient. You could check email from any computer. You didn't need to set up clients on multiple machines. You didn't need to manage storage and downloads. It just worked. And as broadband internet became standard, the connectivity concern evaporated. As companies started offering more and more storage, the local storage argument disappeared. The advantages of desktop email just kept getting smaller.

By 2004, when Gmail launched, the outcome was already inevitable. Google didn't kill desktop email. Gmail just delivered the final blow to something that was already dying. Eudora's fate was sealed the moment webmail became practical. Which means it was sealed in the late 1990s, though nobody acknowledged it at the time.

## What Qualcomm Got Right and Why It Still Didn't Matter

Qualcomm's business model decisions were actually quite good. The three-tier system worked. Free users who later paid. Corporate users who needed features. Students who became corporate users. The Sponsored tier created a revenue stream even when people didn't pay. From a pure business perspective, this was sound. And it worked. Eudora's revenue trajectory was upward through the 1990s and into the early 2000s.

The problem was that they were optimizing for a market that was disappearing. All the revenue in the world doesn't matter if the category you're dominating is being disrupted. This is the trap that every incumbent faces. You can be the best in a category. You can be profitable. You can be growing. And then the category itself becomes irrelevant, and all of your advantages become liabilities.

Sega faced this with arcades. Kodak (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kodak-digital-camera-bankruptcy.html) faced this with film. Blockbuster (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-blockbuster-still-open-last-store.html) faced this with video rental. Eudora faced this with desktop email. Dominance in an obsolete market is just a slow decline. You're still winning, right until you're not winning anymore. And by then, it's too late to reposition.

## The Legacy: Eudora Defined What Email Should Be

Despite being completely forgotten by the general public, Eudora's influence on email design is massive and ongoing. Everything you expect from email, Eudora probably invented or popularized. Threading. Search. Filters. Spam handling. Organization. Conversation views. These seem obvious now because Eudora made them obvious. But they weren't obvious in 1988. Steve Dorner figured these things out and built them into Eudora, and every email system since has borrowed from that template.

Gmail's interface looks nothing like Eudora's, but Gmail's functionality is basically Eudora's design philosophy implemented for the web. Which is maybe the highest compliment you can pay a product: the category evolved to reflect your design decisions, even though everyone forgot you were the one who made them.

The Computer History Museum has Eudora's source code now. It sits there as a historical artifact, a reminder of when a company could own a category completely and still become irrelevant because the category itself became irrelevant. That's the real lesson of Eudora. Not that they made bad decisions. But that being the best at something that's becoming obsolete is the worst position you can be in.

## The Business Model Mismatch: Charging for Software That Wanted to Be Free

One of the fundamental challenges Eudora faced was philosophical. The email client market wanted to move toward free. Outlook Express was free because it came with Windows. Netscape Navigator had an email client and it was free. The open source email clients were free. And then Eudora was charging $49.95 for Eudora Pro, or asking people to look at advertisements if they wanted the free version.

This positioned Eudora as a premium product in a market that was increasingly skeptical of premium pricing for commodity software. In 1995, when email was still somewhat exotic, people would pay $49.95 for a good email client. By 2000, when email was becoming ubiquitous, charging for email software seemed almost offensive. Why pay when you could get something free?

The Sponsored tier with advertising tried to bridge this gap, but advertising in software was becoming increasingly unpopular. People didn't like ads in their operating system. They didn't like ads in their applications. The ad-supported model worked for some software categories, but for something as personal as email, most users wanted it ad-free or free, not ad-supported. This left Eudora in an impossible position: charge for it and lose users to free alternatives, or offer it ad-supported and watch users complain about the ads.

## Why Microsoft's Bundling Strategy Was So Devastatingly Effective

When Microsoft bundled Outlook Express with Windows 95, they weren't trying to destroy Eudora specifically. They were just including an email client with their operating system. But the effect was devastating. Every Windows computer came with an email client. Every computer manufacturer installed Windows. Every user who turned on a new computer saw Outlook Express sitting there, ready to use, with no need to install anything or pay any money.

This is the power of platform bundling. You don't need to make the best product. You just need to make a good enough product and bundle it with something that everyone needs. This strategy worked for Internet Explorer against Netscape. It worked for Outlook Express against every competing email client. And it set the stage for why Gmail, built on the platform of the web, would eventually dominate.

Qualcomm couldn't compete with this strategy because they weren't a platform company. They made software. They sold it to users. Microsoft was a platform company that used their platform to distribute software. Those are different games, and the platform company has structural advantages that a software company can't overcome. Eudora could be better than Outlook Express. It didn't matter. Outlook Express was already there. Already free. Already the default.

## The Email Wars Were Fought on Three Different Battlefields and Nobody Noticed

The decline of Eudora actually happened across three distinct technology shifts, and it's easy to get confused about which one actually killed it. First, there was the shift from bundled email to free email clients. Outlook Express beat Eudora here because Microsoft could bundle for free. Second, there was the shift from desktop to webmail. Hotmail beat desktop clients because webmail didn't require installation. Third, there was the shift from free webmail to useful webmail. Gmail beat Hotmail and other webmail providers because Gmail actually worked well.

Eudora lost on the first battlefield. If they'd won there, they might have competed on the second. If they'd won on the second, they couldn't have competed on the third, because Gmail's advantages were in web infrastructure, not client software. But the first loss was decisive. Once Outlook Express had the installed base, Eudora's advantages evaporated. The trajectory was set. It just took a decade to complete.

## The Open Source Attempt Was Noble and Doomed

When Qualcomm released Eudora as open source under the Penelope project, it was a genuinely interesting decision. They're acknowledging that the market for commercial email clients is gone. They're trying to keep the product alive through community contribution. They're being generous with intellectual property. And it failed completely, which tells you something about markets: open source only works when there's a market demand for the category. Nobody wanted an open source desktop email client because nobody wanted a desktop email client anymore.

The code was good. The product was still useful. But useful for a category that nobody cared about anymore is just irrelevance with good code. By 2010, when the open source effort was basically dead, Gmail had already won definitively. There was no market to capture. No users waiting to switch. No developers interested in maintaining a platform that was already obsolete.

Eudora's story ends not with a bang but with a museum donation. The Computer History Museum has the source code, preserved like all artifacts from eras that have fully passed. It's a fitting end. Not destroyed. Not forgotten. Just archived, with the understanding that this was important once, and now it's history.

## FAQ: Questions About Eudora

Q: Was Eudora really used by 18 million people?

A: Yes, by December 1996. This was measured as installed base, not daily active users. But even accounting for that, Eudora had genuinely achieved dominant market position in desktop email clients. It was the clear market leader by a significant margin.

Q: Why didn't Eudora pivot to webmail?

A: Qualcomm did invest in webmail offerings, but they were always secondary to the desktop client. By the time they fully committed to webmail, Gmail had launched with better technology, better design, better infrastructure, and better funding. They couldn't compete. Sometimes being the leader in the previous category doesn't help you compete in the new one.

Q: Could Eudora still exist today?

A: Theoretically, yes. Thunderbird, which is based on the same Mozilla framework that the open source Eudora attempted to use, still exists and still has users. But nobody wants to use desktop email clients anymore. The ecosystem has moved entirely to web and mobile. A desktop-only email client can't compete with that reality.

Q: What made Eudora better than Outlook Express?

A: More features, better interface design, better search, better filtering, better organization tools. Outlook Express was simpler, which was sometimes an advantage. But Eudora was more powerful. The problem was that "simpler and free" beat "more powerful and paid" when the market had already shifted to webmail, which was even simpler.

Q: Did Steve Dorner continue working on email software after Eudora?

A: Dorner continued leading Eudora development at Qualcomm for many years. When desktop email clients became obsolete, so did the role. The transition from being the most important email software developer in the world to having an obsolete skill set happened very quickly.

# Is SimCity Still Playable in 2026? Yes, From $4.99

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-simcity-ea.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-08  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Gaming, Business Blunders

**Summary:** SimCity still exists as an Electronic Arts property, and the old games still run. SimCity 4 Deluxe Edition lists at $19.99 on Steam and GOG, SimCity 3000 Unlimited at $4.99, and the 2013 reboot has worked offline since March 2014. What does not exist is a new SimCity: EA has not shipped a mainline entry since the 2013 launch that helped close the studio behind it.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: 1989, by Maxis, founded by Will Wright and Jeff Braun in 1987
- Owner today: Electronic Arts, taken private in August 2026 by a consortium led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund
- Last mainline game: SimCity, released 5 March 2013
- Price today: SimCity 4 Deluxe Edition $19.99, SimCity 3000 Unlimited $4.99, SimCity BuildIt free on mobile
- Status today: Franchise dormant on PC, alive on mobile through SimCity BuildIt

## Who owns SimCity today?

SimCity belongs to Electronic Arts, and Electronic Arts itself changed hands in 2026. The company agreed on 29 September 2025 to be taken private by a consortium of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners in a deal worth $55 billion.

Shareholders approved the buyout on 22 December 2025 at $210 a share. The transaction closed in August 2026, and the stock stopped trading on Nasdaq. Under the new structure the Public Investment Fund holds 93.4 percent of Electronic Arts, Silver Lake 5.5 percent and Affinity Partners 1.1 percent.

So the SimCity trademark, the source code and every Maxis game built on it now sit inside a privately held Electronic Arts. Day to day, nothing about the franchise moved. Maxis still exists as an Electronic Arts studio label, and its work goes into The Sims (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/original-sims-best-selling-pc-game.html) rather than city building. SimCity has had no new mainline release since 2013, and no successor has been announced.

## How a rejected city simulator became a franchise

Will Wright and Jeff Braun founded Maxis in 1987 in California to publish a game nobody else would take: a city simulator with no enemies, no score and no way to win. SimCity arrived in 1989, and players zoned land, laid roads and power lines, set tax rates and watched simulated citizens react.

It sold one million copies by late 1992, split evenly between home computers and the Super Nintendo port. SimCity 2000, released in 1993, moved the grid to an isometric view and added terrain elevation, underground water pipes and arcologies. It sold an estimated 4.23 million copies worldwide, still the high-water mark for the series.

SimCity 3000 followed in 1999 and SimCity 4 in 2003, the latter adding regions where several cities shared commuters and resources. By then the studio was no longer independent. Electronic Arts acquired Maxis in a stock swap that valued it at $125 million, completing the deal on 28 July 1997. Wright stayed 12 years, leaving in April 2009 to run Stupid Fun Club, a think tank Electronic Arts co-owned.

## What broke at the SimCity launch in March 2013?

After SimCity 4 the series went quiet for a decade. When Electronic Arts and Maxis brought it back on 5 March 2013, the new game required a permanent internet connection, even for one player alone. The servers could not carry the load.

Buyers could not log in. Those who did lost cities, lost hours and were disconnected mid-game. On 7 March 2013 Amazon (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-amazon-survived-dot-com-crash.html) suspended the digital download and posted a warning to customers, a step The Register reported the same day. Review sites including Polygon and Kotaku held back final scores and published rolling updates instead.

Lucy Bradshaw, general manager of the Maxis label, offered every buyer a free game from the Electronic Arts catalog and wrote in a March 2013 blog post that the gesture was "a little contrived", adding: "But we feel bad about what happened."

The sales were not the problem. An Electronic Arts press release on 18 March 2013 reported more than 1.1 million copies sold in the first two weeks, the biggest SimCity launch to that date, and by July 2013 the company put the figure above 2 million. The reputation was the problem.

## Was the always-online requirement ever necessary?

Maxis had spent months arguing that the new GlassBox engine pushed part of the simulation onto its servers, so offline play was impossible by design. Players tested that claim within days.

A modder using the name UKAzzer forced the game into a developer mode that stopped it quitting when the connection dropped, then played on with no server at all. The Register wrote up the hack on 14 March 2013. A Maxis developer speaking anonymously to Rock Paper Shotgun in 2013 was blunter: "The servers are not handling any of the computation done to simulate the city you are playing."

That left the online requirement looking like digital rights management with a design story wrapped around it, and the trust never came back. Electronic Arts conceded the point a year later. Update 10, released on 18 March 2014, added an offline single-player mode at no extra cost, with regions saved locally and no cap on save files. It is the reason the 2013 game still runs on a modern machine today, the same way you can run 90s PC games on Windows 11 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/run-90s-pc-games-windows-11.html) once the original online check is gone.

## Why did EA close Maxis Emeryville in 2015?

On 4 March 2015, two years and a day after the launch, Electronic Arts shut the Emeryville studio that had built SimCity, SimCity 2000, The Sims and Spore. Maxis designer Guillaume Pierre broke the news himself on Twitter that day: "Well it was a fun 12 years, but it's time to turn off the lights and put the key under the door."

The company framed it as a reshuffle rather than a retreat. Its March 2015 statement read: "Today we are consolidating Maxis IP development to our studios in Redwood Shores, Salt Lake City, Helsinki and Melbourne locations as we close our Emeryville location." The Sims work carried on at the surviving sites, and the Maxis name survived with it. The studio with the institutional memory did not.

The timing was cruel in one more way. Cities: Skylines, built by Colossal Order and published by Paradox Interactive, shipped on 10 March 2015, six days after the closure. It sold more than 250,000 copies in 24 hours and passed one million by 14 April 2015, offering the deep, offline, moddable city builder that SimCity buyers had expected two years earlier.

## What does SimCity cost now, and will there be a new one?

SimCity 4 Deluxe Edition, the version most long-time players still recommend, lists at $19.99 on both Steam and GOG and drops to a few dollars in seasonal sales. SimCity 3000 Unlimited came to Steam on 7 March 2024 at $4.99. SimCity BuildIt, the free mobile entry launched in 2014, is the only part of the franchise still getting new content in 2026.

A new mainline SimCity is a different question. Electronic Arts has announced nothing, Maxis is staffed around The Sims, and the city-building audience it once owned now belongs to Cities: Skylines and its sequel. Anyone hoping for a revival is waiting on a privately held publisher with no stated plan for the series.

Where to find one today: the practical route is digital. SimCity 4 Deluxe Edition runs about $19.99 at list and closer to $4 on sale, and the GOG release is DRM-free, which matters for a 2003 game you want to keep working. Boxed copies of SimCity 2000 and SimCity 3000 still turn up in collectors' hands, but the discs expect hardware that has not shipped in twenty years. Start with the SimCity titles on GOG (https://www.gog.com/en/games?query=simcity). For the broader story of studios that outlived their owners, see RollerCoaster Tycoon (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-rollercoaster-tycoon.html).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is there a new SimCity game in 2026?

No. As of September 2026 the last mainline SimCity is the 2013 release, and Electronic Arts has announced no successor. The only SimCity title still receiving updates is SimCity BuildIt, the free mobile game launched in 2014.

### Who owns SimCity now?

SimCity is owned by Electronic Arts, which bought Maxis in 1997 in a stock swap valuing the studio at $125 million. Electronic Arts was itself taken private in August 2026 in a $55 billion buyout led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners, so the fund holds 93.4 percent of the company that owns SimCity.

### Why did SimCity 2013 fail?

SimCity launched on 5 March 2013 requiring a permanent internet connection, and the servers collapsed under demand. Within nine days a modder had the game running offline, undercutting the claim that server-side computing was necessary, and Electronic Arts added an official offline mode on 18 March 2014.

# Who Owns RollerCoaster Tycoon Now? Atari Publishes It

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-rollercoaster-tycoon.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-08  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Gaming, Software & Apps

**Summary:** RollerCoaster Tycoon is still an active franchise in 2026. Chris Sawyer, who wrote 99% of the 1999 original in x86 assembly language, still holds the trademark, and Atari publishes the series under a long-term licence from him. A new entry, RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks, enters Steam early access in winter 2026 at $24.99.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: March 22, 1999 in North America, Hasbro Interactive under the MicroProse label
- Created by: Chris Sawyer, with graphics by Simon Foster and music by Allister Brimble
- Owner today: Chris Sawyer holds the trademark; Atari publishes under licence
- Status today: Active. RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks in Steam early access, winter 2026
- Price today: RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic $19.99 on Steam; Wonderworks $24.99 in early access

## How one programmer built a theme park in machine code

Chris Sawyer wrote RollerCoaster Tycoon almost entirely in x86 assembly language, the instruction set a processor runs directly, at a point when nearly every commercial PC game was written in C or C++. His own FAQ at Chris Sawyer Software Development gives the split exactly: the game is "99% written in x86 assembler/machine code, with a small amount of C code used to interface to MS Windows and DirectX."

Assembly trades readability for control. A routine that takes ten lines of C can take fifty or a hundred lines of assembly, and the programmer allocates registers and memory by hand. Sawyer had been writing it since the 1980s and carried years of his own tested routines forward from project to project, so the slow language was, for him, the fast one.

The payoff showed on screen. The game tracked hundreds of individual guests, each with hunger, thirst, happiness and its own pathfinding, while running ride physics and scrolling a detailed isometric park on a consumer Pentium. Sawyer did not do everything: Simon Foster drew the graphics and Allister Brimble composed the music.

## How well did RollerCoaster Tycoon actually sell?

Hasbro Interactive released the game in North America on March 22, 1999 under the MicroProse label, the same label that had published Sawyer's Transport Tycoon in 1994. There was no large marketing campaign behind it.

It sold anyway. RollerCoaster Tycoon moved more than 700,000 copies in the United States during 1999 and took about $19.6 million in revenue that year. By July 2002 it had passed four million copies sold. Sawyer posted on his own website in January 2000 that it had finished 1999 as the top-selling PC game of the year.

The money behind those numbers only became public when the franchise ended up in court. Reporting on Sawyer's 2005 claim against Atari put the series' total revenue at roughly $180 million, of which about $30 million had already gone to Sawyer in royalties. For a title with one programmer, one artist and one composer, that is an extraordinary split. The Sims (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/original-sims-best-selling-pc-game.html), the PC game that eventually overtook it, was built by a full Maxis team.

## Why Chris Sawyer took Atari to court

Sawyer commissioned a forensic audit of his royalties in 2003. It concluded he was owed $4.8 million more than he had been paid, and in 2005 he sued Atari in the United Kingdom. Engadget reported the claim on November 8, 2005.

Atari counter-claimed in 2006, arguing it had in fact overpaid Sawyer by $1.6 million. That claim was dismissed in 2007. The two sides settled out of court in 2008 and the terms were never published.

The case matters for a reason beyond the money. Sawyer never sold the property. The rights to the games he designed stayed with him personally, which is why every RollerCoaster Tycoon release since has been somebody else publishing his trademark rather than owning it.

## What went wrong with the games made without Sawyer

Sawyer wrote RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 himself, again in assembly, and Infogrames published it in North America on October 15, 2002. For the third game he stepped back to a consulting role. Frontier Developments built RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 in full 3D and Atari published it on November 2, 2004. It was a real technical leap, and it was the last entry the series' creator had any hand in.

What followed was worse. RollerCoaster Tycoon 4 Mobile arrived in April 2014 as a free-to-play build full of in-app purchases, made without Sawyer. It holds a Metacritic score of 35 from 13 critic reviews. Chris Schilling of Eurogamer scored it 1 out of 10 in 2014 and called its music "irredeemably bad".

RollerCoaster Tycoon World, developed by Nvizzio Creations and published by Atari on November 16, 2016, went the same way: about 26% of its roughly 1,980 Steam user reviews are positive. Frontier Developments released Planet Coaster the same year, and for most players that was the sequel the series never officially got.

## Is RollerCoaster Tycoon still being made in 2026?

Yes, and 2026 is the franchise's busiest year in a decade. Atari and the studio Springloaded announced RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks at gamescom Opening Night Live on August 25, 2026. It enters Steam early access in winter 2026 at $24.99, with console versions planned after the full release. Wade Rosen, chairman and chief executive of Atari, said in the announcement: "RollerCoaster Tycoon is a franchise that has deep meaning to fans, many of whom have played these games for a decade or more."

Ownership sits in two pieces. Chris Sawyer holds the RollerCoaster Tycoon trademark and the rights to the games he designed, and Atari (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-atari-now.html) publishes the series under what it describes as a long-term licensing agreement with him. Atari bought the publishing rights to RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 from Frontier Developments on April 2, 2024 for up to $7 million, $4 million up front and $3 million deferred, in a deal covering eight titles in the series. In November 2024 Sawyer sold Atari the Transport Tycoon intellectual property outright.

The back catalogue keeps moving as well. RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic, the rebuild of the first two games, reached Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in May 2026, after launching on PC in September 2017 and on Nintendo Switch in December 2024.

## How to play the original RollerCoaster Tycoon today

Three routes work in 2026. RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic is the maintained version, a rebuild of the first two games that carries the RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 expansion packs; it lists at $19.99 on Steam and runs on current consoles. RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe and the RollerCoaster Tycoon 2: Triple Thrill Pack are the original 1999 and 2002 builds, repackaged to install on modern Windows, and they are the cheapest way in when the series goes on sale.

The third route is OpenRCT2, a free open-source re-implementation of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 that adds higher resolutions, multiplayer and modern window handling. It is not a standalone game. It needs the data files from a copy of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 or RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic, so you buy the old game and run the new engine on top of it. For anyone who would rather run a 1999 disc as it shipped, the same methods that run 90s PC games on Windows 11 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/run-90s-pc-games-windows-11.html) apply here too.

Where to find one today: the digital versions are the sensible option, because the 1999 CD-ROM needs a working optical drive and a patch before it will start. RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe and the Triple Thrill Pack are sold DRM-free and both fall to a few dollars in seasonal sales. Browse the RollerCoaster Tycoon listings on GOG (https://www.gog.com/en/games?query=rollercoaster+tycoon).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Who owns RollerCoaster Tycoon now?

Chris Sawyer still owns the RollerCoaster Tycoon trademark and the rights to the games he designed. Atari publishes the series under a long-term licensing agreement with him, and bought the publishing rights to RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 from Frontier Developments in April 2024 for up to $7 million.

### Is there a new RollerCoaster Tycoon game in 2026?

Yes. RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks, developed by Springloaded and published by Atari, was announced on August 25, 2026 and enters Steam early access in winter 2026 at $24.99. Console versions are planned after the full release.

### Was RollerCoaster Tycoon really written in assembly language?

Yes. The FAQ on Chris Sawyer's own site says the 1999 RollerCoaster Tycoon is "99% written in x86 assembler/machine code, with a small amount of C code used to interface to MS Windows and DirectX." Simon Foster drew the graphics and Allister Brimble wrote the music.

- Steam: RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks: https://store.steampowered.com/app/4734550/RollerCoaster_Tycoon_Wonderworks/

# Newgrounds Is Still Online in 2026, 31 Years Later

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-newgrounds.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-08  Updated: 2026-09-18
Topics: Internet Culture, Music & Entertainment

**Summary:** Newgrounds is still online in 2026 and still independent, more than 31 years after Tom Fulp founded it on July 6, 1995. Founder Tom Fulp and three staff run it from Glenside, Pennsylvania, with no investors and no parent company. Adobe killed Flash on December 31, 2020, but the archive survived through the Newgrounds Player and the Ruffle emulator, and the site now pays its bills with supporter subscriptions starting at $5 a month.

**Key facts:**
- Status today: Online and independent in 2026, 31 years after launch
- Launched: July 6, 1995, by Tom Fulp, from a 1991 paper fanzine
- Owner today: Newgrounds, Inc., never sold, no outside investors
- Who runs it: Tom Fulp and three staff in Glenside, Pennsylvania
- Cost today: Free to use; Supporter from $5 a month or $36 a year (2026)

## How did a 13-year-old's Neo Geo zine turn into a website?

Newgrounds started on paper. In 1991 Tom Fulp, then 13, published a Neo Geo fanzine called New Ground from his parents' basement in Perkasie, Pennsylvania, and mailed sporadic issues to around 100 members of a club on the Prodigy (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-prodigy-online-service.html) online service.

In 1995 Fulp got his own web space and carried the name online as New Ground Remix. Newgrounds counts July 6, 1995 as its founding date, which made July 6, 2025 its thirtieth birthday as a website.

The turn came in 1998, when Fulp started experimenting with Macromedia Flash. After a call from the TV show Inside Edition about his game Assassin, he registered a domain that would be easy to remember on screen and paid $33 a month out of pocket to host it. "In 1998, I picked up Flash and my life changed forever," Fulp writes on the Newgrounds about page.

Traffic grew faster than the money. By 1999 his host wanted more than $1,000 a month and his only good ad company had dropped him over the site's content, so Fulp partnered with the film studio Troma, which hosted Newgrounds in exchange for a cut of ad revenue. That arrangement lasted until February 2003.

## What actually came out of the Portal?

The Portal started in 1999 as a page where Fulp dumped small projects and then began hosting other people's Flash files, each one hand coded into its own HTML page. On April 6, 2000, Newgrounds automated it. By the site's own account it was the first website anywhere to allow instant self-serve publishing for movies and games, four and a half years before YouTube launched.

That single change turned a personal showcase into a career pipeline. Fulp's Pico's School (1999) became the reference point for what Flash 3 could do. Alien Hominid, built with artist Dan Paladin in 2002, started as a Portal game; the two formed The Behemoth on April 1, 2003, and the console version reached stores in November 2004. The studio's follow-up, Castle Crashers, arrived on Xbox Live Arcade in August 2008. "In the 11 years since its launch, the game has sold over 20 million copies," The Behemoth wrote in 2019.

Animation did the same thing. Salad Fingers, Eddsworld and the Madness series all grew inside the Portal, and the Numa Numa Dance premiered on Newgrounds on December 6, 2004, a full year before YouTube opened. The Audio Portal followed in 2003 so musicians could be credited in other people's work, and an Art Portal arrived in June 2009. Much like Homestar Runner (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/homestar-runner-still-updating.html), the site proved that a small crew could hold an audience without a network behind it.

## When did Newgrounds peak, and what knocked it down?

The clearest peak markers are bandwidth bills. Newgrounds went from a 100mbps cap to 300mbps during 2003, was consuming 500mbps by the end of 2004, and blew past 800mbps during peak hours in December 2005. Time ranked it among the 50 best websites of 2010.

Two things ended that run. The first was video. YouTube made watching easier than the SWF format ever would, and by 2012 Fulp described a site where his own efforts were not changing the trajectory and everyone was, in his words on the history wiki, "livin' la vida YouTube."

The second was ad blocking. Newgrounds ran a 2009 experiment showing banners only to ad block users, which mostly made them angry. "we would go on to lose well over half our revenue to adblock," Fulp wrote on the Newgrounds history wiki, "and it's a big reason why you guys don't get to have nice things." A 2013 peering dispute between Verizon and Cogent, the site's bandwidth provider, throttled it further. Plenty of contemporaries did not survive that stretch at all, as the shutdown of GeoCities (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/history-of-geocities-websites.html) showed.

## What happened when Adobe killed Flash?

Adobe set the date years in advance and hit it. "Flash will be completely removed from all browsers by December 31, 2020, via Windows Update," Microsoft told administrators in its lifecycle notice in 2020. Adobe began blocking Flash content from running on January 12, 2021, which Fulp called the true end of Flash day.

Newgrounds had been preparing since 2011, when staffer Mike built Swivel to convert SWF files to video. In April 2019 the site shipped Newgrounds Player, a desktop application that keeps Flash content playable, with support for medals, high scores and shared creations. In August 2019 it introduced Ruffle, an open-source Flash emulator written in Rust, and started switching classic content over to it in 2020.

The migration is still running. Ruffle gained working medals and high scores for ActionScript 2 games in October 2020, picked up Flash video support in October 2021, and pushed into ActionScript 3 from 2023, after which Newgrounds switched on emulation for thousands more games in the second half of 2024. Newgrounds put $6,000 into Ruffle development in 2021 alone. The full story of the format is in the history of Macromedia Flash (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/definitive-history-macromedia-flash.html).

The archive survived, and so did the audience. Friday Night Funkin' debuted on Newgrounds on November 1, 2020, and when its Week 7 update landed on April 18, 2021 the site broke its one-day record with 1.2 million views on a single piece of content. The game's Kickstarter, launched the same day, raised more than $2 million.

## Who runs Newgrounds in 2026?

Tom Fulp does, and he never sold. Pages across the site carry a Newgrounds, Inc. copyright line reading 1995 to 2026, and the staff page lists him as founder and guy in charge alongside three others: senior programmers Josh Tuttle, who joined in 2008, and James Holloway, who joined in 2002, plus staff artist Jeff Bandelin, who joined in 2006. The company works out of Glenside, Pennsylvania, in a building Fulp bought in 2005.

"Newgrounds has been self-sustained since its inception, free of investor and corporate interests," Fulp writes on the about page. There is no parent company and no acquisition anywhere in the site's history.

The recent work is unglamorous. A large denial-of-service attack in September 2025 led to a screening layer called NG Guard, and the site added age verification for United Kingdom users to comply with the Online Safety Act. Fulp's own summary of 2026 on the history wiki is that overhauls and regulatory compliance remain the heavy themes, alongside a mobile refresh in May 2026. He is still making games too, including a long-delayed console project called Nightmare Cops.

## How does Newgrounds pay for itself now?

Mostly through readers, and not comfortably. Newgrounds launched its Supporter upgrade in September 2012 at $25 for a year of ad-free browsing. It took until Thanksgiving 2018 to reach 2,000 active supporters, a jump helped by Tumblr (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-tumblr-yahoo-billion-dollar-mistake.html)'s ban on adult content, which sent more than 1,000 new artists to the Art Portal within days.

The numbers have improved without solving the problem. "We finished the year with nearly 5,800 Supporters but NG continued to run at a loss," Fulp wrote in the 2021 entry of the history wiki, in a year when the site also sent more than $40,000 to the community in prizes and drawing tablets. In October 2024 Newgrounds added Takeover Tuesday, which lets each supporter feature one item on the front page each week.

In 2026 the pitch is a monthly subscription starting at $5 or a yearly one from $36, which works out to $3 a month paid up front. The site still runs a small amount of advertising on A-rated games and movies. Fulp's stated targets on the history wiki are to "stop losing money, keep increasing the monthly prizes and gradually phase out the last remaining ads." Monthly creator prizes passed $5,000 for the Best of June 2026.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Newgrounds still active in 2026?

Yes. Newgrounds is online and publishing new games, animation, art and music in 2026, more than 31 years after Tom Fulp founded it on July 6, 1995. The site ran its eleventh annual Pixel Day on January 23, 2026 and its sixth annual Flash Forward game jam that spring.

### Can you still play old Flash games on Newgrounds?

Yes. Adobe Flash Player reached end of life on December 31, 2020, but Newgrounds runs its classic archive through Ruffle, an open-source Flash emulator it began sponsoring in 2019, and offers Newgrounds Player, a desktop application released in April 2019, for content Ruffle cannot handle yet. Thousands more games were switched over to Ruffle in the second half of 2024.

### Who owns Newgrounds?

Newgrounds is owned by Newgrounds, Inc., the private company founded by Tom Fulp, who still runs it from Glenside, Pennsylvania. It has never been acquired and has no outside investors, and the staff page listed four people in 2026.

**Sources:**
- Newgrounds Wiki: About Newgrounds: https://www.newgrounds.com/wiki/about-newgrounds
- Newgrounds Wiki: History: https://www.newgrounds.com/wiki/about-newgrounds/history
- Support Newgrounds (Supporter pricing and perks): https://www.newgrounds.com/supporter
- Microsoft Lifecycle: Adobe Flash end of support on December 31, 2020: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/lifecycle/announcements/adobe-flash-end-of-support
- The Behemoth: Castle Crashers Remastered Has Arrived (2019): https://blog.thebehemoth.com/2019/09/17/castle-crashers-remastered-has-arrived/

# Is BonziBuddy Still Around? Gone From PCs in 2004

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-bonzibuddy-spyware.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-08  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Software & Apps, Internet Culture

**Summary:** BonziBuddy is not around anymore. Bonzi Software discontinued the purple gorilla assistant in 2004, after a class action over its fake Windows alerts and a $75,000 Federal Trade Commission penalty for collecting children's data without parental consent. Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi still hold the name, and bonzi.com has pointed at a BonziBUDDY NFT page since February 2022.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: 1999, Bonzi Software Inc. (California)
- Status today: Discontinued in 2004; no supported download
- Owner today: Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi, who now run 2KDirect
- FTC penalty: $75,000 civil penalty, February 2004 (COPPA)
- Detected as: Adware:Win32/BonziBUDDY, Microsoft Defender

## What was BonziBuddy and what did it actually do?

BonziBuddy was a free desktop assistant released in 1999 by Bonzi Software Inc., a California company run by two brothers, Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi. It lived on the Windows desktop, told jokes, ran web searches, read email aloud and offered shopping tips, all in a synthesized voice.

The program was built on Microsoft Agent, the same animated-character framework behind Clippy (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-clippy-microsoft.html) in Microsoft Office. The first release borrowed Peedy, a green parrot from Microsoft's stock character set. In May 2000 Bonzi Software swapped in a character of its own: a purple gorilla named Bonzi.

The Federal Trade Commission described the product plainly in its February 2004 complaint, calling BonziBUDDY "intelligent agent software that displays an interactive, animated purple gorilla on the desktop of users' computers." The basic version, the complaint noted, was free.

Free was the whole business model. In 1999 there was no common vocabulary for software that earned its keep from your attention and your browsing history, so the gorilla arrived before anyone had built defenses against it.

## Why did security researchers call BonziBuddy spyware?

Because of what it installed and changed without a clear ask. BonziBuddy reset the browser homepage to bonzi.com, added an Internet Explorer toolbar, tracked what users did online and served its own advertising. Taking it off a machine was harder than putting it on.

In 2002 Consumer Reports Web Watch labeled BonziBuddy spyware, one of the first mainstream consumer verdicts on a category that barely had a name yet. Antivirus vendors followed, and the classification stuck.

It still holds in 2026. Microsoft's malware encyclopedia lists the program as "Adware:Win32/BonziBUDDY", and Microsoft Defender removes it on sight. That is a rare thing: a 1999 consumer product with a live threat-database entry more than two decades later.

The defense at the time was the license agreement, which disclosed some of the data collection. Almost nobody read it. The gap between what a user thought they had agreed to and what the agreement actually permitted is the whole story of desktop adware in the early 2000s, and BonziBuddy sat at the center of it, alongside file-sharing clients like Kazaa (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kazaa-p2p-wars.html).

## What did the fake Windows alerts cost Bonzi Software?

Bonzi Software bought banner space across the web and styled the ads to look like Windows system dialogs. They ran headers such as "security alert" or "warning", told visitors their IP address was being broadcast, and used close buttons that did not close anything.

A class action was filed against the company on December 4, 2002. ClickZ reported in 2003 that the suit accused Bonzi of a "diabolical scheme" that tricked internet users into clicking through to its site.

The case settled on May 27, 2003. Under the terms, Bonzi Software agreed to put the word "Advertisement" in the header of any online ad that resembled a computer system warning and on the pages those ads led to, and to stop using fake close buttons. ClickZ reported that the company paid the plaintiffs' firm, Lukins & Annis, $170,000 in legal fees, made no damages payment, and settled before the class was certified.

The remedy, in other words, was a label. That was roughly the ceiling of consumer protection for deceptive web advertising in 2003.

## Why did the FTC fine Bonzi Software $75,000?

Children. The BonziBUDDY registration form asked for a birth date along with other personal details, and the complaint filed for the FTC on February 17, 2004 in the Central District of California said Bonzi Software had actual knowledge that thousands of children under 13 were registering. Under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, in force since April 2000, that triggered a duty to give parents direct notice and obtain verifiable consent. Bonzi Software did neither.

The company agreed to pay $75,000 in civil penalties. The same FTC announcement carried a $400,000 penalty against UMG Recordings, at that point the largest COPPA civil penalty on record.

The Bonzi case mattered well beyond the money. The FTC called it "the first COPPA case to challenge the information collection practices of an online service in connection with a software product." Enforcement until then had been aimed at websites and their registration forms. The purple gorilla extended the statute to anything you downloaded.

A second action followed that year. On September 1, 2004 Bonzi Software and its two principals settled FTC charges over InternetALERT, a security product sold at $49 for a one-year subscription and advertised as cutting the risk of internet attacks. The FTC said the software "provides only limited protections for computers and the information stored in them," and the consent order required the company to notify subscribers and offer prorated refunds.

## Who owns BonziBuddy today?

Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi still control the name. Bonzi Software stopped distributing BonziBuddy in 2004, the download lingered on bonzi.com into 2005, and the portal itself went dark later that decade. The brothers moved on to 2KDirect, a San Luis Obispo advertising company that sells online campaigns to small businesses and is still trading in 2026.

The domain came back in February 2022, pointed at an OpenSea page selling BonziBUDDY NFTs credited to the original creators. That is the closest thing to an official BonziBuddy product now. There is no supported download, no company selling the assistant and no vendor to complain to.

What circulates instead is fan work: mirrors of the final 2004 build, a browser chat site called BonziWORLD that volunteers have rebuilt several times, and repackaged "safe" builds on itch.io with the advertising and tracking code stripped out. The original servers have been offline for about two decades, so the program cannot phone home. It is still adware by every antivirus definition, and Microsoft Defender will still quarantine it.

For anyone who wants the character without the risk, a video or one of the browser recreations is the sane route in 2026, the same way people revisit Microsoft Bob (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-microsoft-bob-friendly-interface.html) without installing it.

## What did the BonziBuddy cases change?

Three things, and only one of them was about a gorilla.

First, after February 2004 the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act was no longer a website rule. Any downloadable program that asked a child for a birth date and an email address sat inside the statute, which is why later enforcement reached games and mobile apps rather than sign-up pages.

Second, the September 2004 InternetALERT order put marketers on notice that a security promise is an advertising claim, and that the FTC will ask what the software actually blocks.

Third, the 2003 settlement made an "Advertisement" label the baseline for anything dressed up as a system message. Dark patterns did not disappear. Cookie walls, buried cancellation flows and notification prompts styled like alerts are all descendants. What became legally expensive was the specific trick of a banner pretending to be Windows telling you that you were under attack.

The lasting part is the question BonziBuddy forced into the open and nobody has answered. What does consent mean when the user and the software maker know very different things about what the software is doing? In 1999 the answer was a license agreement nobody read. In 2026 it is a privacy policy nobody reads.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is BonziBuddy a virus?

BonziBuddy is not a virus, because it did not copy itself from machine to machine. It is classified as adware and spyware: it changed the browser homepage to bonzi.com, installed a toolbar, tracked browsing and served ads. Microsoft's malware encyclopedia still lists it as Adware:Win32/BonziBUDDY, and Microsoft Defender removes it in 2026.

### Can you still download BonziBuddy in 2026?

There is no official BonziBuddy download in 2026. Bonzi Software discontinued the program in 2004 and the bonzi.com download disappeared in 2005. Copies of the final build circulate on fan mirrors and repackaged versions exist on itch.io, but antivirus software flags the original as adware, so most people use browser recreations such as BonziWORLD instead.

### Who made BonziBuddy?

BonziBuddy was made by brothers Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi through their California company, Bonzi Software Inc., which released the assistant in 1999 and gave it the purple gorilla character in May 2000. After the 2003 advertising settlement and the 2004 FTC actions, the brothers moved on to 2KDirect, a San Luis Obispo online advertising firm.

**Sources:**
- FTC: UMG Recordings to Pay $400,000, Bonzi Software to Pay $75,000 to Settle COPPA Civil Penalty Charges (2004): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2004/02/umg-recordings-inc-pay-400000-bonzi-software-inc-pay-75000-settle-coppa-civil-penalty-charges
- United States v. Bonzi Software, Inc., FTC complaint (February 17, 2004): https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/cases/040217compbonzi.pdf
- FTC: Software Company's Protection Promises Fall Short (September 2004): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2004/09/ftc-charges-software-companys-protection-promises-fall-short
- ClickZ: Bonzi Settles Deceptive Ad Suit (2003): https://www.clickz.com/bonzi-settles-deceptive-ad-suit/85292/
- Microsoft Security Intelligence: Adware:Win32/BonziBUDDY: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Adware%3AWin32%2FBonziBUDDY

# Is The Sims 1 Still Playable in 2026? Yes, $19.99

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/original-sims-best-selling-pc-game.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Gaming, Software & Apps

**Summary:** The Sims 1 is still playable in 2026. Electronic Arts reissued the February 2000 original as The Sims: Legacy Collection on January 31, 2025, bundling the base game with all seven expansion packs for $19.99 on Steam, the EA app and the Epic Games Store, patched to run on Windows 10 and 11. The franchise has passed 200 million copies sold, and EA itself has been privately owned since August 4, 2026 by a consortium led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

**Key facts:**
- Released: February 4, 2000, by Maxis and Electronic Arts
- Status today: Sold as The Sims: Legacy Collection since January 31, 2025
- Price today: $19.99 list on Steam, the EA app and the Epic Games Store
- Owner today: Electronic Arts, private since August 4, 2026 under a PIF-led consortium
- Franchise sales: More than 200 million copies across all Sims games

## Why did Maxis almost cancel the Dollhouse project?

Will Wright lost his house in the Oakland firestorm of October 1991. Rebuilding it meant months of floor plans, budgets and furniture catalogs, and he started treating the whole ordeal as a system: constraints, trade-offs and people whose needs collided with the rooms they lived in.

He began prototyping in 1993 under the internal name Dollhouse. Management at Maxis, the studio he co-founded and the company behind SimCity (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-simcity-ea.html), did not want it. Co-founder Jeff Braun summed up the room in four words that Chaim Gingold recorded in his 2024 MIT Press history Building SimCity: “A dollhouse? That's for little girls.”

The market research went no better. Maxis tested the concept on teenage boys, the demographic the industry assumed bought every game. Wright later described the result to the games historian Jimmy Maher, whose 2026 Digital Antiquarian history of Maxis quotes him: “This was probably the most negative focus-group experience I have ever seen.”

By the mid-1990s Maxis was in trouble financially, and the project was shelved. For several years the game that would outsell every PC title before it did not officially exist.

## How did Electronic Arts end up rescuing the game?

Electronic Arts acquired Maxis in 1997, mainly for SimCity. What EA also got was Wright and a cancelled life simulator nobody had been able to explain in a sales meeting.

The rescue is the part that sounds backwards today, when EA is better known for closing studios than saving their strangest projects. PC Gamer put it plainly in its 2025 write-up of the episode: Maxis had killed The Sims, and EA brought it back. The publisher funded the team, kept the design intact and shipped the game on February 4, 2000 for Windows.

Expectations were modest, because the game fit no shelf category. It had no win condition, no final level and no opponent. Players furnished a house, filled it with people, and kept them fed, employed and on speaking terms with each other. The marketing problem that had almost killed it turned out to be the product: there was nothing else like it on the shelf.

It was the best-selling PC game of 2000, and it stayed at the top of the PC charts for years afterward while the industry's attention moved to the PlayStation 2 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/playstation-2-best-selling-console-ever.html) and the Xbox.

## How many copies did the original Sims sell?

By March 22, 2002, The Sims had sold more than 6.3 million copies worldwide and passed Myst, the 1993 Broderbund adventure game that had held the record for best-selling PC game since the CD-ROM era began. By February 2005, the base game had shipped about 16 million copies.

The expansion packs did the rest. EA released seven of them between August 2000 and October 2003: Livin' Large, House Party, Hot Date, Vacation, Unleashed, Superstar and Makin' Magic. Each one added careers, locations or systems, and the cumulative effect was a game that by 2003 looked nothing like the one that shipped in 2000.

The sequel confirmed the scale of the audience. The Sims 2 arrived on September 14, 2004 and sold a million copies in its first ten days, the biggest PC launch EA had recorded to that point. Counting every sequel, expansion and console port, the franchise has now passed 200 million copies sold, which keeps it among the best-selling series in the industry.

## What made the game reach people who never bought games?

In 2000, PC game marketing was aimed almost entirely at young men. The Sims broke that assumption in public. Electronic Arts has estimated that women make up as much as 60 percent of Sims players, a share no other blockbuster PC game of that period came close to.

Those players built things. The modding scene appeared within months, years before Steam Workshop made mods a one-click install. People downloaded zip files of custom furniture, wallpaper and character skins from fan sites and dropped them into game folders by hand, the same way PC players of the era kept RollerCoaster Tycoon (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-rollercoaster-tycoon.html) alive with homemade scenery.

The darker half of the appeal became the most durable meme in the series. Sims could not climb out of a swimming pool without a ladder, because the pathfinding required an exit tile. Delete the ladder while a Sim is swimming, and the Sim eventually drowns. It was never a designed feature, and players found it almost immediately.

That was the real engine of the game. Nothing scripted a story, so every story came out of systems colliding: a burnt dinner, a kitchen fire, a firefighter, a new romance. Two decades of life sims have tried to reproduce that, and very few have.

## Who owns The Sims today?

Electronic Arts still owns The Sims, but EA itself changed hands in 2026. On August 4, 2026, a consortium of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners completed a $55 billion take-private of the publisher, paying shareholders $210 a share and delisting the stock from the Nasdaq. PIF holds about 93 percent of the company.

The studio name survived better than the studio. EA closed the Maxis office in Emeryville, California in March 2015 and moved the work to other sites. Will Wright left EA in April 2009, more than a decade before the buyout, and has had no role in the series since.

The current game is The Sims 4, free to download since October 18, 2022, with EA selling expansion packs, game packs and kits on top of it. EA reported 85 million players in March 2024. In its January 2026 franchise update, the company described its long-rumored next project, Project Rene, as “a social, collaborative, mobile-first life-sim game” and said again that it is not the successor to The Sims 4. There is no Sims 5 on any published schedule.

## What does it cost to play the original in 2026?

EA put the first two games back on sale on January 31, 2025. The Sims: Legacy Collection lists at $19.99 and includes the base game plus all seven expansion packs; The Sims 2 Legacy Collection lists at $29.99 with its eight expansions and stuff packs. Both are sold on Steam, the EA app and the Epic Games Store, and both were patched to install and run on Windows 10 and 11 without the compatibility workarounds fans had relied on for a decade. Storefront sales have cut both to $14.99 during 2026.

That matters because the 2000 CD-ROM release does not install cleanly on a modern machine. If you own the discs and want to try anyway, the same tools that help with running 90s PC games on Windows 11 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/run-90s-pc-games-windows-11.html) apply here.

Where to find one today. Sealed and complete big-box copies of the 2000 release and its expansions are collector items now and trade in the tens of dollars, more for clean boxes with the manual and the cardboard insert. For the rest of that era's PC catalog, restored and DRM-free, the usual home is GOG's classic PC game store (https://www.gog.com/en/games), though EA sells The Sims itself only through its own three storefronts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can you still play the original Sims in 2026?

Yes. Electronic Arts reissued the 2000 game as The Sims: Legacy Collection on January 31, 2025, with all seven expansion packs included and patches for Windows 10 and 11. It sells for $19.99 on Steam, the EA app and the Epic Games Store, and has been discounted to $14.99 during 2026.

### Who owns The Sims now?

Electronic Arts owns The Sims and has since it acquired Maxis in 1997. EA is no longer a public company: a consortium of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners completed a $55 billion buyout on August 4, 2026, with PIF holding roughly 93 percent.

### How many copies has The Sims sold?

The original Sims passed 6.3 million copies in March 2002, which made it the best-selling PC game to that date, ahead of Myst, and had shipped about 16 million copies by February 2005. Across every sequel, expansion and console version since 2000, the Sims franchise has sold more than 200 million copies.
