# Is Polaroid Still in Business? The Brand in 2026

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-polaroid-camera.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Hardware, Then vs Now

**Summary:** Polaroid still exists in 2026, but not as the Massachusetts company that invented instant film. The original Polaroid Corporation filed for bankruptcy in 2001 and its successor filed again in December 2008; the brand and the film now belong to the Smolokowski family through Polaroid B.V., a Dutch company. Its plant in Enschede is the only factory on Earth still making Polaroid film, and a pack of eight shots costs about $19.

**Key facts:**
- Founded: 1937 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by Edwin Land
- First camera: Model 95, November 26, 1948, $89.75 at Jordan Marsh in Boston
- Status today: Still trading; cameras and film sold worldwide
- Owner today: The Smolokowski family, through Polaroid B.V. in the Netherlands
- Price today: About $19 for eight i-Type shots in 2026, close to $2 a picture

## What did Edwin Land actually invent in 1948?

Polaroid Corporation was founded in 1937 by Edwin Land, a Harvard dropout who had made his name in light-polarizing filters. The instant camera came later, and it started with a question. On a 1943 family holiday in Santa Fe, Land's three-year-old daughter Jennifer asked why she could not see the photograph he had just taken of her.

Land had an answer five years later. On November 26, 1948, the Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 went on sale at the Jordan Marsh department store in Boston for $89.75. The store had 57 cameras in stock. All 57 sold on the first day, along with every pack of film that went with them.

What the Model 95 did was collapse a week into a minute. Before it, a roll sat in the camera until it was finished, went to a drugstore, and came back days later. If the exposure was wrong, or someone blinked, the photographer found out then. Land's system developed the negative and the print together inside a sealed sandwich of reagents, and 60 seconds later the picture was in the owner's hand.

## Why was the SX-70 such a big deal in 1972?

Land spent two decades chasing the version he really wanted: no timing, no peeling, no chemical-coated negative to throw away. He showed it at Polaroid's annual meeting on April 25, 1972, where he called it "absolute one-step photography", as Fast Company recounted in 2022 on the camera's fiftieth anniversary.

The SX-70 folded flat enough for a coat pocket, opened into a single-lens reflex camera in chrome and leather, and pushed out a white square that developed in the open air while its owner watched. Each frame carried more than a dozen engineered layers that had to fire in sequence, at room temperature, without a darkroom anywhere in the process.

It also fixed the shape of everything Polaroid sold afterwards. The white square frame became the brand, more recognizable than the company's logo. Andy Warhol, Ansel Adams and Walker Evans all worked with Polaroid materials, which gave the format a standing in galleries that ordinary consumer film never had.

## Why did Polaroid miss digital photography?

Not for lack of research. Polaroid ran a serious electronic imaging program through the 1980s, and by 1989 digital imaging accounted for close to 42% of the company's research and development spending, according to the study Mary Tripsas and Giovanni Gavetti published through Harvard Business School in 2000. Working sensors and prototypes existed years before Polaroid shipped a digital camera in 1996.

What the company lacked was a reason to want one. Polaroid sold cameras near cost and made its margin on film, which ran around 65% gross. Every digital picture was a picture that earned the company nothing, so senior management kept treating electronic imaging as a front end bolted onto a film business. The engineers lost that argument for a decade.

The warning had already come and gone. Polavision, Land's instant home movie system, launched in 1977 into a market Betamax (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/betamax-vs-vhs-format-war.html) and VHS had taken first, and Polaroid wrote down about $68 million on it in 1979. Land gave up the chief executive job in 1980, left the board in 1982, and died in 1991 holding 535 patents. Kodak (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kodak-digital-camera-bankruptcy.html) made the same mistake on a larger scale, and for the same reason.

## How did Polaroid go bankrupt twice?

Revenue peaked at about $3 billion in 1991 and slid through the decade as one-hour photo labs, then cheap digital cameras, took the casual snapshot market. On October 11, 2001, Polaroid Corporation filed for Chapter 11 protection carrying roughly $950 million in debt, one month after September 11 and with no buyer waiting.

The sale took ten months. In June 2002 a bankruptcy judge approved the transfer of the business to One Equity Partners, the private equity arm of Bank One, for $255 million in cash plus about $200 million in assumed trade liabilities, as CFO magazine reported. Executives who ran the company into bankruptcy collected bonuses. Around 6,000 retirees lost the lifetime benefits they had been promised.

The second collapse was uglier. Minnesota businessman Tom Petters bought the Polaroid name in 2005, and in December 2008 the companies he controlled, Polaroid among them, went into bankruptcy as federal investigators unwound his fraud. Petters was sentenced in 2010 to 50 years in prison for a Ponzi scheme prosecutors put at $3.65 billion. By then the Polaroid badge was turning up on televisions and DVD players, the same licensing afterlife Atari (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-atari-now.html) has lived through.

## Who owns Polaroid today?

Polaroid is a Dutch company now. When the last film plant, in Enschede in the Netherlands, closed in 2008, two men who met at the closing event bought its machinery for about $3.1 million and leased part of the building: Austrian collector Florian Kaps and the plant's production manager, Andre Bosman. They named it the Impossible Project after a line of Land's that Bloomberg Businessweek quoted in 2016: "Don't undertake a project unless it's manifestly important and nearly impossible."

The machines came with no formulas. Polaroid's chemistry was proprietary and several key suppliers had shut down, so it took two years to make film that worked at all. The first packs shipped in 2010, muted and slow and unpredictable, and the people who had been hoarding expired film in their refrigerators bought them anyway.

The money came from the Smolokowski family, Polish investors who took a stake in 2012 and bought the Polaroid brand itself in May 2017. Film maker and trademark ended up in the same hands: the business trades as Polaroid B.V., the trademarks sit in PLR IP Holdings, and the name went from Polaroid Originals back to plain Polaroid in March 2020. The Enschede plant is still the only factory on Earth making Polaroid film, with close to 140 employees.

## Is instant film worth buying in 2026?

Instant photography stopped being a niche some time ago. Fujifilm announced in April 2025 that its Instax line had passed 100 million cameras and printers sold since 1998, and Polaroid has held the expensive, heritage position beside it instead of competing on price.

The economics are the same ones Land set in 1948: the camera is cheap, the film is not. A Polaroid Now Generation 3, released in March 2025, sells for about $130, and the small Polaroid Go starts nearer $80. A pack of eight i-Type color shots runs about $19 in 2026, close to $2 per picture. That per-shot number, not the camera price, is what the decision actually rests on.

What $2 buys is one physical object that cannot be duplicated, deleted or scrolled past, which is the whole appeal to buyers who have never known a world without a camera in their pocket. Old prints are a separate problem with a cheaper answer: scanning photos and negatives (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/scan-old-photos-negatives-2026.html) costs a fraction of a dollar per image, well under the price of shooting new ones.

## Where to find a vintage Polaroid camera today

Original SX-70 bodies still work when the electronics and the light seals do, and both fail with age. Professionally refurbished chrome SX-70s from specialist restorers start around $399 in 2026. Untested bodies from flea markets and estate sales cost far less and usually need a service, which is worth pricing before buying one. Condition notes and seller history matter more than the listing photograph here, which is why vintage Polaroid cameras on Etsy (https://www.etsy.com/search?q=vintage+polaroid+sx-70+camera) are an easier place to start than an unlabeled box at a market. Check which film the body takes before paying: 600 and i-Type packs are made today, while several older pack formats have not been produced for years, and budget about $2 a shot on top of whatever the camera costs.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Polaroid still in business in 2026?

Yes. The Polaroid that exists in 2026 is Polaroid B.V., a Dutch company that grew out of the Impossible Project, and it sells instant cameras and film worldwide. The original Polaroid Corporation of Cambridge, Massachusetts filed for bankruptcy in October 2001, and the successor company that carried the name filed again in December 2008.

### Who owns Polaroid now?

Polaroid has belonged to the Smolokowski family since May 2017, when the Polish investors behind the Impossible Project bought the brand. They hold the trademarks through PLR IP Holdings and run the business as Polaroid B.V., which makes every pack of Polaroid film at its factory in Enschede, the Netherlands.

### How much does Polaroid film cost in 2026?

A pack of eight Polaroid i-Type color shots costs about $19 in 2026, close to $2 per photograph, and 600-format film for older Polaroid cameras costs roughly the same. The cameras are the cheaper half: a Polaroid Go starts near $80 and a Polaroid Now Generation 3 sells for about $130.

# Who Owns Iomega Now? The Zip Drive Click of Death

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-iomega-zip-drives.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Hardware, Then vs Now

**Summary:** Iomega is no longer in business as an independent company. EMC Corporation bought it in April 2008 for about $213 million, the brand was replaced by LenovoEMC in 2013, and that product line was discontinued in 2018, so what is left of Iomega now sits inside Dell Technologies. The Zip drive the company was built on launched in March 1995 at $199, shipped more than 21 million units by 1998, and was undone by the Click of Death defect and by cheap CD-RW and USB storage.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: March 1995, $199 drive and $19.95 100MB disks
- Peak value: Nearly $7 billion, May 1996
- Drives shipped: More than 21 million by fiscal 1998
- Owner today: Dell Technologies, through EMC's 2008 purchase
- Status today: Brand retired; the LenovoEMC line ended in 2018

## What did an Iomega Zip drive cost in 1995?

Iomega shipped the Zip 100 in March 1995 at $199 for the drive, with 100MB disks at $19.95 each. A standard floppy disk (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/floppy-disks-still-made-today.html) held 1.44MB, so one Zip disk did the work of roughly seventy of them.

The company behind it was not new. Iomega was founded on April 1, 1980 in Roy, Utah, and spent the 1980s selling the Bernoulli Box, a removable cartridge drive introduced in 1982 that found buyers in publishing and CAD work but never in living rooms.

The Zip drive was the first Iomega product a college student could afford. Design files, project folders and early MP3 collections moved between machines on one cartridge, at a time when email attachments were capped at a few megabytes and CD burners were studio equipment.

Sales followed at once. Iomega reported $362 million in revenue in 1995, the launch year. By the fiscal 1998 annual report it filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company counted more than 21 million Zip drives shipped.

## How did Iomega reach a $7 billion valuation?

Kim Edwards became president and chief executive of Iomega in January 1994 and backed the Zip project. The numbers that followed were the kind Wall Street builds legends on.

Revenue went from $362 million in 1995 to $1.2 billion in 1996, and to $1.7 billion in 1997, the figure Forbes used in its 1998 profile of Edwards. Market value moved the same way, from roughly $300 million in 1995 to nearly $7 billion by May 1996.

Iomega became one of the most heavily traded stocks of the mid-1990s and an early case of retail-investor mania, years before anyone used the phrase meme stock. Message boards traded tips on it the way they would trade tips on anything else twenty years later.

The peak did not hold. Edwards resigned under pressure in 1998, shortly after Iomega said it would report a first-quarter loss, ending a four-year run in which annual sales had gone from under $150 million to more than a billion. It is the same shape of story as Kodak losing the market it invented (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kodak-digital-camera-bankruptcy.html), compressed into three years instead of thirty.

## What caused the Zip drive Click of Death?

The phrase was in print by January 1998. A failing Zip drive made a steady click as its read/write head hunted for track zero, struck its end stops, and came back misaligned.

The mechanism was cheap and clever. A linear actuator slid the head along a single thin steel rod on two sleeve bearings, and a small doughnut-shaped foam washer at the end of that rod cushioned the stop when power was cut. On drives built over a period of several months, that washer was left out to save production cost.

Without it, a sudden stop could damage the fragile suspension holding the head. A damaged drive then wrote bad alignment onto a disk, and that disk could misalign the head in the next drive it was pushed into. The fault spread from machine to machine, which is what turned an ordinary manufacturing defect into a story.

Steve Gibson of Gibson Research Corporation documented the problem in 1998 and reached a blunt conclusion: "Since the true cause of Click Death is a physically, electrically, or mechanically defective Zip or Jaz drive, the only possible 'cure' is the replacement of that drive."

## Did Iomega get sued over the Click of Death?

Yes. A class action was filed in 1998 in the Superior Court of the State of Delaware, New Castle County, as Rinaldi v. Iomega Corp. The plaintiffs alleged that the drives and disks carried "a manufacturing and/or design defect" that caused failures and destroyed stored data.

Iomega's public position was that the problem was rare. By early 1999 the company said the Click of Death had affected "fewer than half of 1 percent of all Jaz and Zip users." Owners who had lost a thesis or a client's artwork did not find that figure reassuring.

The settlement arrived in 2001. As the Deseret News reported in April of that year, every United States customer who bought a Zip drive between January 1, 1995 and March 19, 2001 became eligible for rebates on Iomega products, plus free technical support for clicking problems and a donation of Iomega products and services to schools. Iomega admitted no wrongdoing.

The scale was unusual for a consumer hardware case. Plaintiffs' counsel said the suit involved more than 150,000 Iomega technical documents, and the class reached as many as 28 million Zip drive buyers.

## What replaced the Zip drive?

Cheaper optical media came first. A blank CD-R held 650 to 700MB and read in any CD-ROM drive, and once CD-RW burners hit consumer prices in the late 1990s, a 100MB cartridge stopped making sense.

Iomega's own filings track the fall. Sales of Zip products were $984.8 million in 2000, down 18.1 percent from $1,202.6 million in 1999. Zip drive revenue alone fell 19.7 percent to $571.7 million, with units shipped down 27.8 percent. The company attributed the drop to lower Zip and Jaz sales, partly offset by its own CD-RW business.

Bigger cartridges did not rescue it. The Zip 250 arrived in 1999 at $199 and the Zip 750 in 2002 at $180, both after the market had moved on. USB flash drives then removed the last reason to own one: no drive to install, no cartridge, no clicking.

It was the trap that also caught Sony's MiniDisc (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-minidisc-sony.html). A proprietary cartridge with a licensing model loses to an open disc that costs pennies, however good the engineering is.

## Is Iomega still in business in 2026?

No. Iomega does not exist as an independent company, and no product sold in 2026 carries the name. EMC Corporation announced its purchase on April 8, 2008: a cash tender offer of $3.85 a share, worth about $213 million, folding Iomega into a new consumer and small business division.

The name survived five more years. In 2013, EMC's joint venture with Lenovo rebranded the remaining network storage line as LenovoEMC, and that line was discontinued in 2018. EMC itself merged with Dell in 2016, so whatever is left of Iomega sits inside Dell Technologies today.

The hardware outlasted the company. Wikipedia dates the Zip range from 1995 to 2003, while the Museum of Obsolete Media puts the end of the Zip 250 and Zip 750 at 2006.

Where to find one today. Working Zip hardware still circulates among collectors: USB and parallel port externals, internal ATAPI units, and sealed boxes of 100MB disks. Buy a drive with its original power supply and cable, because the externals use a specific adapter and a bare unit is close to useless without it. Sellers list both drives and media on Etsy (https://www.etsy.com/search?q=iomega+zip+drive). Prices move with interface and condition rather than with any fixed rate, so compare several listings, and treat an untested drive as a gamble given the defect above.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is Iomega still in business in 2026?

Iomega is not in business as an independent company in 2026. EMC Corporation bought Iomega in April 2008 for about $213 million, the brand was replaced by LenovoEMC in 2013, that product line was discontinued in 2018, and EMC merged with Dell in 2016, leaving the remnants inside Dell Technologies.

### What was the Zip drive Click of Death?

The Click of Death was a failure mode in Iomega Zip drives, named in print by January 1998, in which a misaligned read/write head struck its end stops and clicked. A defective Zip drive could damage a disk, and that disk could then misalign the head in the next drive, so the fault spread between machines.

### How much did an Iomega Zip drive cost?

The Iomega Zip 100 drive launched in March 1995 at $199, with 100MB Zip disks at $19.95 each. Iomega later sold the Zip 250 in 1999 for $199 and the Zip 750 in 2002 for $180, both after CD-RW burners had undercut the format.

# Does Kazaa Still Exist? The P2P Network in 2026

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kazaa-p2p-wars.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Software & Apps, Internet Culture

**Summary:** Kazaa no longer exists. The free file-sharing network ended after Sharman Networks settled with the recording industry for $115 million in July 2006, and the licensed Kazaa subscription service that replaced it went dark in August 2012 when its operator, Atrinsic, filed for bankruptcy. No Kazaa client has been maintained since.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: March 2001, by the Dutch company Consumer Empowerment
- Peak: 229,513,316 downloads by May 2003, a Download.com record
- Settlement: $115 million paid to the recording industry, July 2006
- Status today: Shut down; the licensed service stopped in August 2012
- Owner today: None active. Atrinsic held the license and filed for Chapter 11 in June 2012

## Who built Kazaa, and why did it survive Napster's shutdown?

Kazaa Media Desktop appeared in March 2001, released by Consumer Empowerment, a Dutch company run by Niklas Zennstrom of Sweden and Janus Friis of Denmark. The software sat on top of FastTrack, a peer-to-peer protocol written by the Estonian programmers of BlueMoon Interactive, a team headed by Jaan Tallinn, who had sold the technology to Zennstrom and Friis.

The timing was everything. Napster (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-napster-now.html) ran every search through its own servers, so when a United States court ordered those servers switched off in 2001, the whole network went dark in a single move. FastTrack had no center to switch off. It promoted well-connected machines on the network to supernodes, each holding a searchable index of files on the peers around it and answering their queries. Shut one down and the network simply routed around it.

That one design decision is why Kazaa, rather than any of the dozen other clients launched in 2001, inherited the audience Napster left behind. It also set the legal problem that would define the next five years: there was no plug to pull, so the recording industry had to go after the company, the users, or both.

## How big did Kazaa get, and what did it install on your computer?

In late May 2003, Kazaa Media Desktop passed ICQ (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-icq-instant-messenger.html) to become the most downloaded piece of software tracked by CNET's Download.com, with 229,513,316 cumulative downloads. That spring the FastTrack network was peaking at close to four million people online at the same moment, which made it the largest file-sharing network in the world by a wide margin.

It was free because it was not really free. The installer came bundled with advertising software, and depending on the version, with tracking components that most users never read about in the license agreement. Advertising paid for the network. For a reader in 2002 that trade looked reasonable: albums for nothing, in exchange for pop-ups.

Quality control did not exist. A file labeled as a hit single might be the song, a badly encoded copy, a different track entirely, or a virus. The Recording Industry Association of America turned that weakness into a weapon, flooding the network with corrupted decoy files so that finding a clean copy took several tries. Sorting real results from fake ones became a skill of its own, and it pushed experienced users toward BitTorrent and LimeWire (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-limewire-file-sharing.html) well before the courts caught up.

## Why did the record labels sue tens of thousands of ordinary people?

On September 8, 2003, the Recording Industry Association of America started suing individual file sharers. One of the first defendants was Brianna LaHara, a twelve-year-old living in a Manhattan housing project, who had just started the seventh grade. Her family settled within days for $2,000.

"I am sorry for what I have done. I love music and don't want to hurt the artists I love," LaHara said in a statement carried by TechNewsWorld in 2003. Her mother added that the family had not understood the software was illegal. The case did more to shape public opinion than any of the thousands that followed.

The strategy was never to sue everyone. It was to make the risk feel personal. Settlement demands typically landed around $3,000, far less than fighting would cost, so almost nobody fought. The Hollywood Reporter counted roughly 35,000 lawsuits against individuals by the time the recording industry stopped filing them in late 2008 and turned to working with internet providers instead. The campaign changed behavior and cost the labels years of goodwill doing it.

## What did the Australian court decide about Sharman Networks?

By 2002 the Kazaa application belonged to Sharman Networks Limited, a company incorporated in Vanuatu and run from Sydney by Nikki Hemming, with the FastTrack protocol licensed in from Joltid Ltd. Hemming said the Vanuatu incorporation was for tax reasons. The entertainment industry read it as a deliberate effort to put the company out of reach of any single court.

It did not work. In Universal Music Australia Pty Ltd v Sharman License Holdings Ltd, decided in the Federal Court of Australia on September 5, 2005, Justice Murray Wilcox found that the respondents had "authorised" Australian users to "make a copy of the sound recordings" and to "communicate the recordings to the public". The finding turned on knowledge: Sharman knew what the network was mostly used for, had technical means available to filter copyrighted files, and chose not to use them because filtering would have cut its own revenue.

On July 27, 2006, Sharman Networks settled with the recording industry worldwide for $115 million, with more than $100 million of it going to Universal Music, Sony BMG, EMI and Warner Music. Sharman also agreed to turn Kazaa into a licensed service and to build in measures against piracy. "Kazaa was an international engine of copyright theft which damaged the whole music sector and hampered our industry's efforts to grow a legitimate digital business," said John Kennedy, then chief executive of the IFPI, in Billboard in 2006.

## Who owns Kazaa now?

Nobody is operating it. After the settlement the Kazaa name passed to Brilliant Digital Entertainment, the Sydney company run by Kevin Bermeister, which relaunched Kazaa in July 2009 as a paid subscription service with tracks licensed from the four major labels. In October 2010 the service was taken over by Atrinsic, a New York digital marketing firm, which put out a Kazaa app for the iPad in March 2011.

The second life lasted under two years. Atrinsic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the Southern District of New York on June 15, 2012, saying it had shut down its direct-to-consumer subscription business and could not raise more working capital. The Kazaa site stopped serving anything that August. No maintained Kazaa client has shipped since, no company sells or supports the software in 2026, and the name never got the second life that the LimeWire brand did.

Anything offered today as a Kazaa download is a copy of abandoned 2000s software, shipped by somebody with no connection to Sharman Networks, Brilliant Digital Entertainment or Atrinsic, and usually with the original adware still attached. There is no legitimate version to install.

## What happened to the technology behind Kazaa?

It got a knighthood instead of a sentence. Niklas Zennstrom, Janus Friis and the Estonian engineers who wrote FastTrack reused the same supernode architecture in 2003 to route voice calls, and called the result Skype (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/skype-shut-down-what-replaced-it.html). Microsoft bought it in 2011 and retired it on May 5, 2025, moving the remaining users to Teams.

Jaan Tallinn, who headed the team that wrote the protocol, went on to fund research into risks from artificial intelligence. The code that was treated as a criminal instrument when it moved MP3 files was treated as a breakthrough when it moved voice packets. The architecture never changed. Only the payload did.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does Kazaa still exist in 2026?

No. Kazaa stopped being a free file-sharing network after Sharman Networks settled with the recording industry in July 2006, and the licensed Kazaa subscription service that replaced it went offline in August 2012. No Kazaa client has been maintained since then, and no company operates the service in 2026.

### When did Kazaa shut down?

Kazaa shut down in two stages. The original file-sharing operation ended with the $115 million settlement of July 27, 2006, and the licensed music service that carried the Kazaa name stopped in August 2012, two months after its operator Atrinsic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on June 15, 2012.

### Who created Kazaa and the FastTrack protocol?

The FastTrack protocol behind Kazaa was written by the Estonian programmers of BlueMoon Interactive, a team headed by Jaan Tallinn, who sold it to Niklas Zennstrom and Janus Friis. The two launched Kazaa Media Desktop in March 2001 through their Dutch company Consumer Empowerment, then sold the application to Sharman Networks in 2002.

# Is Club Penguin Coming Back? Who Owns It in 2026

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-club-penguin.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Gaming, Internet Culture

**Summary:** Club Penguin shut down on March 29, 2017, and The Walt Disney Company still owns the trademark and the code. No official version has existed since Club Penguin Island closed on December 20, 2018, so the game runs only on unlicensed fan servers such as Club Penguin Legacy and Club Penguin Journey. Co-founder Lane Merrifield joined Walt Disney Imagineering in May 2026, which restarted the revival rumors, but Disney has announced nothing.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: October 24, 2005, New Horizon Interactive, Kelowna, BC
- Status today: Closed since March 29, 2017; no official version since 2018
- Owner today: The Walt Disney Company, which bought it on August 1, 2007
- Price paid: About $350 million in cash; a further $350 million earnout was never paid
- Peak accounts: More than 200 million registered by July 2013

## How three developers in Kelowna built a penguin world

Club Penguin started as Penguin Chat, a Flash experiment by Lance Priebe, a developer in Kelowna, British Columbia. Instead of a text box, users got a penguin avatar they could walk around a shared screen.

Priebe rebuilt the idea with Lane Merrifield and Dave Krysko under a company called New Horizon Interactive. The new version was aimed squarely at children: filtered chat, paid human moderators, and no practical way to hand out a phone number. Club Penguin entered public beta on August 22, 2005 and launched on October 24, 2005.

The design was a park rather than a chatroom. Penguins walked between rooms, decorated igloos, played small games for coins, adopted puffles and turned up for parties that ran on fixed dates. A free account covered most of it, and a paid membership bought clothing, furniture and member-only rooms. That split is why parents tolerated it and why kids asked for it. The whole thing ran on Adobe Flash (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/definitive-history-macromedia-flash.html), the plugin browsers finally dropped at the end of 2020.

## Why Disney paid $350 million for a two-year-old game

The Walt Disney Company announced the purchase on August 1, 2007: about $350 million in cash, with up to another $350 million payable if Club Penguin hit earnings targets in calendar 2008 and 2009. Coverage at the time put the site at roughly 700,000 paid subscribers and 12 million activated accounts, mostly in the United States and Canada.

Growth continued under Disney. By July 2013 the game had passed 200 million registered accounts, a figure that counts every penguin ever created rather than anyone still logging in.

The second half of the deal never arrived. Disney's Form 10-Q filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in 2009 recorded that Club Penguin missed its 2008 earnings target, cutting $175 million from the purchase price. The 2009 target went the same way, so the full $350 million earnout lapsed and the founders never saw it. Priebe and Merrifield both left the company in the years that followed.

## Why Disney closed the game in 2017

Disney announced the shutdown on January 30, 2017 and set the closing date at March 29, 2017. Memberships stopped selling the next day. The stated reason was a move to mobile: Club Penguin Island, an app-only remake, launched the same week the browser game closed.

People who worked on it describe a different mechanism. Chris Heatherly, the Disney executive who ran Club Penguin, wrote on X in 2024 that when the game was shut down "it was making $30m in revenue a year with a team of 15," and said the business was recorded as losing money only once corporate overhead was assigned to it.

The replacement did not last either. In September 2018 Disney told staff at the Kelowna studio that Club Penguin Island was closing and that they were being laid off, as Variety reported at the time. The servers went off on December 20, 2018, less than two years after launch, and the franchise was left with no official version at all.

## Is Club Penguin still playable in 2026?

Not officially. Disney owns the trademark, the art and the code, and has run no Club Penguin service since December 20, 2018. There is no Disney archive, no offline client and no paid legacy server.

What exists instead is a set of unlicensed fan recreations built from the original assets and a reverse-engineered protocol. Club Penguin Legacy, which is free and takes no memberships or donations, passed 1,000,000 registered penguins on November 3, 2025 and was still running scheduled events in September 2026. Club Penguin Journey, released on February 5, 2023 and built to look like the pre-2013 game, passed 1 million registered players in July 2026 and was the most consistently active server on the penguintrack load tracker in June 2026.

None of that is settled legally. Every one of these servers runs on Disney property and survives only until Disney decides otherwise. Readers who followed the other virtual worlds of the era will recognize the contrast with Habbo Hotel (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-habbo-hotel-still-around.html) and Neopets (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-neopets-virtual-world.html), which both stayed open under their own owners.

## Why the police seized the biggest fan remake

Club Penguin Rewritten launched in 2017, weeks after the original closed, and reported more than 11 million registered accounts by 2022. It was the largest of the recreations and the least discreet about it.

On April 13, 2022 the site went dark and was replaced by a City of London Police seizure notice, following a copyright complaint from Disney. The force's Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit said that "three people were arrested on April 12 on suspicion of distributing materials infringing copyright" and that searches were carried out. The three were released under investigation and signed the website over to police control.

It was not the first action. In 2020 Disney shut down Club Penguin Online, a server that had picked up a large pandemic audience along with serious moderation failures, including racist and sexual content that the operators did not remove. Club Penguin Legacy received a DMCA notice from Disney on January 18, 2023 and closed temporarily on January 24 before returning.

## What Lane Merrifield's move to Imagineering means

In May 2026 Lane Merrifield, the co-founder who handled sales and marketing and was known in game as Billybob, posted that he had started a job at Walt Disney Imagineering. "I got lost ten times trying to find my way around the office, but otherwise it was a pretty magical day," he wrote on Instagram, and Disney fan outlets picked the post up within two days.

That is the entire basis for the revival rumors. Merrifield has not said what he is working on, and Disney has announced no Club Penguin project, rerelease or archive. Imagineering designs attractions and physical experiences rather than browser games, so the plainest reading of the job is theme parks, not a server relaunch.

The property is not forgotten inside Disney. The company defended it in 2020, in 2022 and again in 2023, and a company that keeps sending takedown notices is a company that still values the trademark. That is the same reason an official return stays possible and an unofficial one stays fragile.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When did Club Penguin shut down?

Disney announced on January 30, 2017 that Club Penguin would close, and the browser and app versions shut down on March 29, 2017, with the servers going quiet in the early hours of March 30. The mobile replacement, Club Penguin Island, launched the same week and shut down on December 20, 2018.

### Can you still play Club Penguin in 2026?

There is no official Club Penguin in 2026, because Disney has operated no version of the game since Club Penguin Island closed on December 20, 2018. The game runs only on unlicensed fan servers, among them Club Penguin Legacy, which passed 1,000,000 registered penguins in November 2025, and Club Penguin Journey, which passed 1 million in July 2026. Disney has shut several of these servers down, including Club Penguin Rewritten in April 2022.

### How much did Disney pay for Club Penguin?

Disney paid about $350 million in cash for Club Penguin in a deal announced on August 1, 2007, with up to another $350 million tied to earnings targets in 2008 and 2009. Club Penguin missed both targets, so Disney never paid the second half, and the company's 2009 SEC filing recorded a $175 million reduction in the purchase price for the 2008 miss.

- The Walt Disney Company, Form 10-Q, SEC (2009): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1001039/000119312509017678/d10q.htm

# Is MiniDisc Still Made? Sony Ended Discs in 2025

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-minidisc-sony.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-07  Updated: 2026-09-21
Topics: Hardware, Music & Entertainment

**Summary:** MiniDisc is no longer manufactured. Sony sold the last MiniDisc hardware in March 2013 and announced in January 2025 that it would end production of recordable MiniDisc media the following month, with no replacement. The format now lives entirely in the second-hand market, where a clean recorder runs roughly $100 to $400.

**Key facts:**
- Announced: May 1991 by Sony, first players on sale in Japan in late 1992
- US launch: December 1992, $750 for a recorder
- Status today: Discontinued. Last players sold March 2013, blank discs ended February 2025
- Owner today: Sony still owns the format and the trademark but sells nothing for it
- Price today: About $100 to $400 for a working used recorder

## What problem was MiniDisc built to solve?

Sony spent the late 1980s watching two formats split the job of playing music. The compact disc sounded clean and jumped to any track instantly. The cassette could be recorded at home, over and over, for almost nothing. Neither one did both.

MiniDisc was Sony's answer. It was a magneto-optical disc, rewritable thousands of times, sealed inside a plastic shell so fingers never touched the surface, holding 74 minutes of audio on a disc small enough to lose in a coat pocket. A memory buffer read ahead of the laser so the music kept playing when the player was knocked, which is the one thing portable CD players could never manage.

Sony announced the format at a press conference in May 1991. "We understand consumer needs, and we put our technology to work to meet those needs," said Norio Ohga, then Sony's president and chief executive, in the company's 1991 announcement.

The audio was compressed to fit. ATRAC, Sony's own codec, discarded the sound a listener was least likely to notice was gone. It was good work, and it was lossy, and both of those facts followed MiniDisc for the rest of its life. The first players reached Japanese shops in late 1992 and American ones that December.

## How big did MiniDisc actually get in Japan?

Big enough to beat the CD player on its home turf. Japanese buyers took about 1,080,000 MiniDisc machines and 10 million blank discs in 1995 alone. By 1997, MiniDisc player sales in Japan had overtaken CD player sales, with roughly 5 million units sold there against about 1 million in the United States. Worldwide hardware sales hit 6.3 million units in 1998, alongside 60 million blank discs.

The reasons were local and specific. Japanese commuters spent hours a day on trains, where a skipping portable CD player (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sony-discman-portable-cd-player.html) was a daily irritation. Home recording from rented CDs was normal and legal, and MiniDisc did it faster and cleaner than a cassette deck, with track names typed onto the little screen.

The part that mattered most was content. Japanese record labels pressed albums onto pre-recorded MiniDiscs and sold them next to the CDs, on release day. That closed the loop: music in the format sold players, and players sold labels on pressing more music. No other market ever got that far.

## Why did MiniDisc flop in the United States?

Two numbers explain most of it. A MiniDisc recorder cost $750 at the American launch in December 1992, and Sony sold fewer than 50,000 of them in the first twelve months. Sony aimed the marketing at young music buyers who could not possibly pay $750 for a music player.

American buyers already had an answer that worked. CDs were everywhere, and recordable CD-R blanks were heading toward pocket change. MiniDisc asked them to pay several times as much for a smaller disc that held less and compressed the audio. The only argument that could have won was a rack of pre-recorded albums in the store, and the major American labels never pressed them. They saw a proprietary Sony format, they distrusted the compression, and they had no reason to split a CD market that was printing money.

So MiniDisc stayed where it started: a format for people who recorded their own music. That is a real audience, and a small one. Sony had been on the losing side of this arithmetic before, when Betamax lost to VHS (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/betamax-vs-vhs-format-war.html) on availability rather than quality.

## Did the copy protection drive away the people who wanted it most?

MiniDisc shipped with the Serial Copy Management System. A digital recording made from a CD onto a MiniDisc was allowed. A digital copy of that MiniDisc onto another MiniDisc was not. One generation, then the chain stopped.

Sony built that restriction to reassure record labels, and it mostly annoyed the enthusiasts who were buying the hardware. The people willing to spend real money on a recording format were exactly the people who wanted to move their recordings around freely.

The fixes that followed kept the restrictions. NetMD in 2001 added a USB cable and Sony's SonicStage software, which is the moment MiniDisc started arguing against itself: if the music already lived on a computer, why move it onto a proprietary disc instead of a player that took the files as they were? Hi-MD in 2004 raised the capacity and finally allowed uncompressed recording, which was the right feature several years late. By then the iPod (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/ipod-wasnt-first-mp3-player-heres-why-it-won.html) had already settled the question of where portable music would live.

## Is MiniDisc still made in 2026?

No. Sony sold the last MiniDisc players in March 2013, more than twenty years after the format launched. Blank media outlived the hardware by a decade, because Sony kept pressing recordable discs for the Japanese market long after nobody was selling new decks.

That ended too. On 23 January 2025 Sony announced it would stop producing recordable MiniDisc media, MD Data discs, MiniDV cassettes and recordable Blu-ray the following month. The company's statement left no ambiguity: "There will be no successor models." Production of blank MiniDiscs stopped in February 2025, and since Sony was the last manufacturer, the world now has a fixed and shrinking supply of blank discs.

Ownership has not changed hands. Sony still holds the MiniDisc format and trademark, which makes this different from the brands that got sold off in bankruptcy. Sony simply stopped selling anything for it. What keeps the format usable is community work rather than corporate support: Web MiniDisc Pro, a browser tool built on WebUSB, now does what SonicStage did, without installing Sony's abandoned software on a modern machine.

MiniDisc also turns up in places nobody planned. In June 2019, 18 hours of Radiohead recordings from the OK Computer era leaked after, as guitarist Jonny Greenwood put it to the press that month, "someone stole Thom's minidisk archive from around the time of OK Computer." The band released the whole archive rather than pay the ransom.

## Where to find one today

Only used, and condition is most of the price. A well kept portable recorder typically runs $100 to $400 in 2026, while a unit with a dim display or a grinding transport sells for a fraction of that, because the repair costs more than the player is worth. Most pre-recorded MiniDisc albums still change hands for under $100, though sealed Japanese pressings by major artists have reached four figures at auction. Blank discs keep climbing now that production has stopped. Sellers list players, blanks and pre-recorded discs on Etsy (https://www.etsy.com/search?q=minidisc+player). Test the transport and the headphone output before you commit to anything.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Are MiniDiscs still being made in 2026?

No. Sony announced on 23 January 2025 that it would end production of recordable MiniDisc media in February 2025, and it was the last manufacturer still making them. Sony had already stopped selling MiniDisc players in March 2013, so as of 2026 no new MiniDisc hardware or blank media is being produced by anyone.

### How much does a MiniDisc player cost in 2026?

A working used MiniDisc recorder generally costs $100 to $400 in 2026, depending on the model and its condition, and units with worn transports or failing screens sell for much less. No new MiniDisc players have been built since Sony ended production in March 2013, so every unit on the market is second-hand.

### Does MiniDisc sound as good as a CD?

Standard MiniDisc does not, because it uses Sony's lossy ATRAC compression and permanently discards part of the audio during recording. ATRAC was tuned so that most listeners would not notice the loss on portable equipment, and Hi-MD, which Sony introduced in 2004, did allow uncompressed recording at full CD quality.

- MiniDisc Growth in Japan (MiniDisc.org): https://www.minidisc.org/md_growth.html
- Slate: Remember MiniDiscs? Neither Did We Until Radiohead's Old Recordings Were Hacked (2019): https://slate.com/technology/2019/06/radiohead-minidisc-hack-leak-history.html
- The FPS Review: Sony to End Production of Blu-ray Disc Media, MiniDisc for Recording, and More in February (2025): https://www.thefpsreview.com/2025/01/23/sony-to-end-production-of-blu-ray-disc-media-minidisc-for-recording-and-more-in-february-there-will-be-no-successor-models/
- Headphonesty: The Music Format Everyone Mocked Is Now Selling for Thousands (2026): https://www.headphonesty.com/2026/07/mocked-music-format-selling-thousands/

# Do Screensavers Still Exist? Flying Toasters Today

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-screensavers-flying-toasters.html
Author: Marcus Vale (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-06  Updated: 2026-09-20
Topics: Software & Apps, Then vs Now

**Summary:** Screensavers still exist in 2026: Windows 11 ships six of them and macOS runs Apple's aerial videos when a Mac goes idle. What died was the paid screensaver industry, which peaked with Berkeley Systems at about $30 million a year before the company was sold in 1997. LCD panels removed the burn-in problem that created the whole category.

**Key facts:**
- First screen saver: SCRNSAVE by John Socha, Softalk magazine, December 1983
- Peak of the paid market: Berkeley Systems, about 120 staff and $30 million a year by the mid-1990s
- Status today: Still built into Windows 11 and macOS; the boxed screensaver business is gone
- Owner today: After Dark went to the Sierra On-Line division of CUC International in 1997, with no version sold since
- Price today: SereneScreen Marine Aquarium, $14.95

## What did burn-in actually do to a CRT monitor?

Screensavers began as damage control, not decoration. A cathode ray tube drew its picture by firing an electron beam at a phosphor coating on the inside of the glass, and phosphor that glowed in the same spot for hours aged faster than the phosphor around it.

The result was a permanent ghost. A menu bar, a login prompt or a spreadsheet grid left on screen overnight could still be read with the monitor switched off. Offices suffered most, because a terminal at a bank counter or an airline desk showed the same layout all day, every day.

The cure was to take the bright pixels away. John Socha, later known for Norton Commander, published a program called SCRNSAVE in the December 1983 issue of Softalk. It blanked an IBM PC display after three minutes of inactivity and did nothing else. Socha is also credited with coining the term screen saver.

That was the entire original brief: stop the picture from sitting still. Everything that came later, the toasters and the pipes and the fish, was decoration bolted onto a maintenance task.

## How did a flying toaster become a $30 million business?

Berkeley Systems was founded in Berkeley, California in 1987 by Wes Boyd and Joan Blades, and its first products were access tools for blind Macintosh users. After Dark, the screensaver that made the company famous, was brought to them by two programmers, Jack Eastman and Patrick Beard, and reached the Macintosh in 1989 and Windows in 1991.

The design was modular. Instead of blanking the screen, After Dark ran swappable animated modules and let the owner pick a favorite. Flying Toasters, which arrived with version 2.0 rather than the first release, was the one people bought the box for.

The origin is as small as it sounds. "I drifted into the kitchen, and the toaster caught my eye. My sleep-deprived brain put wings on it," Eastman told Low End Mac in 2007. He drew the frames in the development system's icon editor and gave the toasters what he called "little stubby plucked-chicken wings" and a flapping electrical cord.

By the mid-1990s Berkeley Systems employed about 120 people and was taking in roughly $30 million a year. Boyd and Blades sold the company to the Sierra On-Line division of CUC International in 1997, then went on to found MoveOn.org.

## Why did Microsoft build 3D Pipes in the first place?

3D Pipes was an advertisement. Windows NT 3.5, released in 1994, shipped with OpenGL support, and the team that built it had a presentation problem. As Raymond Chen of Microsoft told the story on The Old New Thing in 2024, "there was nothing in the product that let the user know that this feature even existed".

A full 3D application was too risky that close to release, because a bug in it could hold up the whole operating system. A screensaver was safe. If it fell over, the desktop came back and nothing else was harmed.

So the Windows OpenGL group ran an internal screensaver contest, with the winner to be voted on and shipped. The entries included 3D Text, 3D Flying Objects, 3D Maze and 3D Pipes. Marketing liked them enough that Microsoft shipped all of them instead of just the winner.

Pipes drew an endless branching network of plumbing, changing color at every joint and occasionally using a Utah Teapot as a connector, an in joke aimed at anyone who had sat through a computer graphics course. It stayed in Windows through 95, 98, 2000 and XP, and was removed in Windows Vista.

## Do Windows 11 and macOS still have screensavers in 2026?

Yes, which surprises people who assume the feature was deleted. In Windows 11 it sits under Settings, then Personalization, then Lock screen, then Screen saver. The options are None, Blank, Bubbles, Mystify, Photos and Ribbons, and the default is None.

None of the OpenGL classics came back. Bubbles and Ribbons date from the Windows Vista era, and 3D Pipes, 3D Maze, 3D Text and 3D Flying Objects have never been restored. Windows also ties the setting to sign-in behavior, so picking a screensaver can change when the machine asks for a password again.

Apple went the other way and made the screensaver a selling point. macOS ships the slow motion aerial videos that play on an idle Apple TV, grouped as landscape, cityscape, underwater and earth, and the clip fades into the desktop wallpaper at login.

Burn-in has also come back. OLED panels age unevenly where a static image sits, which is why monitor makers ship pixel shift and panel refresh features and tell owners to leave them on. On an OLED desk monitor, a dark screensaver is once again doing the job it was invented for.

## What killed the paid screensaver market?

Three things, roughly in order. LCD monitors replaced CRTs through the late 1990s and 2000s, and an LCD has no phosphor to burn. It can hold a faint image after a very long static display, but that fades by itself rather than scarring the glass.

Power management finished the job. Rather than run an animation to keep the tube busy, operating systems learned to cut power to the monitor after a set idle period, which saves electricity instead of spending it. Turn off the display replaced run a screensaver as the sensible default.

Then the software became free. Once Windows and the Mac both shipped screensavers in the box, the case for buying a boxed set of animations collapsed. Berkeley Systems had built a $30 million business on a product that operating system vendors proceeded to give away.

The habit died with it. In the 1990s the screensaver you chose was a small piece of office identity, filed next to the desktop wallpaper and the mouse pad. Downloading one from a stranger's website was also a dependable way to end up with something like BonziBuddy (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-bonzibuddy-spyware.html) riding along inside the installer.

## Where can you run After Dark and 3D Pipes today?

After Dark has not been sold as a new product in decades. Berkeley Systems went to Sierra On-Line in 1997, the screensaver line stopped there, and nobody has shipped a new version since, so there is nothing to buy.

The originals survive anyway. The Internet Archive hosts the After Dark releases as downloadable software, and front-end developer Bryan Braun rebuilt Flying Toasters and several sibling modules in pure CSS, so they run in a browser with nothing to install. Community projects have done the same for 3D Pipes and 3D Maze.

For the real binaries on real hardware, the route is the one that works for running 90s PC software on Windows 11 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/run-90s-pc-games-windows-11.html): a virtual machine with a period operating system, which is also the only way to see these modules at the resolution they were drawn for. Most of them were drawn for the desktop that shipped on the night Windows 95 launched (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/the-night-windows-95-launched.html).

One paid screensaver outlived the extinction. SereneScreen Marine Aquarium, written by former Air Force pilot Jim Sachs and first released in July 2000, is still sold and still updated at $14.95. A digital fish tank has now outlasted the entire industry that surrounded it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why did screensavers stop being necessary?

Screensavers existed to prevent phosphor burn-in on CRT monitors, and the LCD panels that replaced CRTs through the late 1990s and 2000s have no phosphor to damage. Operating systems also began switching the display off after an idle period instead of animating it, which saves power rather than using it. OLED panels can age unevenly, so modern monitors handle the same problem with pixel shift and panel refresh instead.

### Who made the Flying Toasters screensaver?

Flying Toasters was a module in After Dark, the screensaver published by Berkeley Systems of Berkeley, California, which reached the Macintosh in 1989 and Windows in 1991. Programmer Jack Eastman drew the winged toasters after a late night walk to his kitchen, as he told Low End Mac in 2007. Berkeley Systems was sold to the Sierra On-Line division of CUC International in 1997 and After Dark has not been sold as a new product since.

### Can you still get 3D Pipes on Windows 11?

Not from Microsoft. 3D Pipes shipped with Windows from NT 3.5 in 1994 through Windows XP, was removed in Windows Vista, and Windows 11 offers only None, Blank, Bubbles, Mystify, Photos and Ribbons. Community recreations of 3D Pipes run in a browser or as a standalone download, and the original still runs inside a virtual machine with a period version of Windows.

**Sources:**
- The origin story of the Windows 3D Pipes screen saver, The Old New Thing (Microsoft), 2024: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20240611-00/?p=109881
- Aggressively Stupid: The Story Behind After Dark, Low End Mac, 2007: https://lowendmac.com/2007/aggressively-stupid-the-story-behind-after-dark/
- Berkeley Systems, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_Systems
- Marine Aquarium, SereneScreen: https://serenescreen.com/about.html
- How to enable screen saver on Windows 11, Windows Central: https://www.windowscentral.com/how-enable-screen-saver-windows-11

# Is Clippy Still Around in 2026? Microsoft's Paperclip

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-clippy-microsoft.html
Author: Dana Reyes (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-06  Updated: 2026-09-20
Topics: Software & Apps, Then vs Now

**Summary:** Clippy, officially named Clippit, has not shipped as a working Microsoft Office feature since Office 2007 stripped out the Office Assistant. The character still exists inside Microsoft software in 2026, as the paperclip emoji in Microsoft 365 since 2021 and as a hidden avatar in the consumer Copilot app since October 2025. It has never come back as an assistant that watches what you type.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: November 19, 1996, in Microsoft Office 97
- Official name: Clippit, drawn by illustrator Kevan Atteberry
- Switched off: Office XP, announced April 11, 2001
- Removed: Office 2007, along with every Office Assistant character
- Status today: Not a feature. A Microsoft 365 emoji and a hidden Copilot avatar

## Why did Microsoft put a cartoon inside Office 97?

The Office Assistant began with academic research rather than marketing. In the early 1990s the Stanford professors Clifford Nass and Byron Reeves ran experiments showing that people apply social rules to computers without meaning to. Praise from a machine made test subjects rate that machine more favorably. Terse, unhelpful responses made them feel snubbed. They called the effect the media equation and published the book of the same name in 1996.

Microsoft drew a product conclusion from it. If users already treated software as a social actor, the reasoning went, software should have a face. The first attempt was Microsoft Bob (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-microsoft-bob-friendly-interface.html), the 1995 release that replaced the Windows desktop with a cartoon house and a guide dog named Rover. Bob was discontinued inside a year.

Alan Cooper, the programmer known as the father of Visual Basic, later argued that the whole concept rested on a "tragic misunderstanding" of the Stanford work. Nass and Reeves had described an unconscious reflex. Microsoft turned it into a specification.

The internal lesson from Bob was not that the premise was wrong but that the scope had been too large. Shrink the character down, put it inside one application instead of the whole desktop, and it might work. That decision produced the Office Assistant, which shipped with Microsoft Office 97 on November 19, 1996.

## How did a paperclip beat 250 other characters?

Illustrator Kevan Atteberry was one of the artists hired to draw candidates. "We designed about 250 characters, and I had about 15 or 20 of 'em in there," he told Mental Floss in 2017. The pool ran from animals and robots to household objects and cartoon humans.

The shortlisting was handed to the same discipline that had inspired the project. Social psychologists from Stanford spent six months putting the designs in front of focus groups, asking members of the public which characters felt trustworthy, likeable and funny. The googly-eyed paperclip finished first on trust, engagement and endearment. Some testers in those sessions still flagged the eyes as leering, and the paperclip shipped anyway.

Its official name was Clippit. Almost nobody used it. Within a year of Office 97 reaching desks the character was Clippy to users, to the press and eventually to Microsoft's own advertising.

Atteberry drew the winner on an Apple Macintosh, a detail he has repeated in interviews for years, and which remains the neatest irony in the story.

## What made Clippy unbearable once real work started?

Clippy was enabled by default, which is the detail that turned a feature into a grievance. Everyone who installed Office 97 got him whether they wanted him or not. Start typing something that pattern-matched to correspondence and he appeared: "It looks like you're writing a letter. Would you like help?"

The complaint was never that help existed. It was that the help arrived unrequested, animated itself to pull your eye away from the document, and rarely matched the problem you actually had. Dismissing him was temporary. He came back.

The focus groups had measured the wrong thing. A test session lasts minutes, and over minutes the paperclip reads as charming. Office work lasts hours, days and years, and the same twitching character reads as an interruption. The research that picked Clippy captured first impressions, not the fiftieth impression.

By 1999 disabling the Office Assistant had become a standard step in corporate PC setup, the same way turning off BonziBuddy (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-bonzibuddy-spyware.html) became standard on home machines a couple of years later. Office was the dominant productivity suite on the planet, so hundreds of millions of people had to learn how to switch off a feature Microsoft had spent years researching.

## How did Microsoft fire its own mascot in 2001?

On April 11, 2001, Microsoft announced that the Office Assistant would be switched off by default in the next release. Then the company did something stranger than a quiet retirement. It made the firing into the marketing campaign.

At the Office XP launch in New York on May 31, 2001, a performer in a Clippit costume interrupted the presentation, begged for his job back and was hauled off the stage by an oversized magnet. Microsoft put up a promotional site, officeclippy.com, carrying three Flash cartoons about an unemployed paperclip looking for work: "Clippy Gets Clipped", "Clippy Goes Undercover" and "Clippy Faces Facts". There was also a Flash game, X-tract Paperclip. Gilbert Gottfried voiced Clippy for the campaign.

Office XP still contained the Assistant in code, just off unless a user went looking. The final cut came with Office 2007, which removed every Office Assistant character. No version of Microsoft Office since has shipped one.

## Where does Clippy still exist in Microsoft software?

Clippy is still around in 2026, but not as anything that helps you write. He survives in two places, both of them decorative.

The first is the emoji set. In July 2021 Microsoft posted a picture of the paperclip with the line, "If this gets 20k likes, we'll replace the paperclip emoji in Microsoft 365 with Clippy." The post cleared 20,000 likes within hours and went on to roughly 175,000, and Microsoft shipped the swap as part of a refresh of about 1,800 emoji across its products. The company later admitted the redesign had already been finished before the vote.

The second is Copilot. In its October 2025 release Microsoft gave the consumer Copilot assistant an animated avatar called Mico, and left Clippy inside it as an easter egg: tap the avatar rapidly, about a dozen times, and it turns into the paperclip. It is a skin over Mico rather than a working assistant, you cannot set it as the default, and it does not appear in Microsoft 365 Copilot, the business version.

Beyond Microsoft, Clippy has had a second life as merchandise and as fan software, which is a better fate than most discontinued features of the Windows 95 era (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/the-night-windows-95-launched.html) managed.

## Why does every AI assistant still get compared to Clippy?

Kevan Atteberry spent years distancing himself from the work. "I would never include Clippy in my portfolio because I was so embarrassed of him," he told The Register in 2023. Ironic nostalgia in the 2010s changed that, and the character that symbolized bad software design became a mascot for retro computing.

The comparison persists because the design problem never went away. Every major software company now ships an assistant that watches your document, anticipates what you want and offers to do it for you. The vocabulary changed from Office Assistant to copilot, and the underlying question from 1996 is unchanged: how does an assistant stay helpful without becoming an interruption?

Clippy answered it by counterexample. Do not turn the assistant on for everyone by default. Do not animate for attention. Do not assume the pattern you matched is the task the user is doing. Modern assistants are better at reading context and much better at staying quiet, and when they get it wrong the insult people reach for is still the name of a paperclip from 1996.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When was Clippy removed from Microsoft Office?

Clippy, officially named Clippit, was switched off by default in Office XP after Microsoft announced the change on April 11, 2001, and every Office Assistant character was removed outright in Office 2007. No version of Microsoft Office released since 2007 has shipped the Office Assistant.

### Who designed Clippy?

Clippy was drawn by the illustrator Kevan Atteberry, who contributed 15 to 20 of the roughly 250 character designs Microsoft tested for the Office Assistant in Office 97. Atteberry drew the paperclip on an Apple Macintosh, and has said he left Clippy out of his portfolio for years because he was embarrassed by it.

### Is Clippy coming back as an AI assistant?

Not as a product. Microsoft's consumer Copilot assistant uses an avatar called Mico, introduced in October 2025, and tapping that avatar repeatedly turns it into an animated Clippy as a hidden easter egg. Clippy has not returned as a working Microsoft Office feature since Office 2007 removed it.

**Sources:**
- Office Assistant, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Assistant
- The Tragic Life of Clippy, Mental Floss (2017): https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/504767/tragic-life-clippy-worlds-most-hated-virtual-assistant
- Clippy creator was 'so embarrassed' after its Office arrival, The Register (2023): https://www.theregister.com/2023/06/12/clippy_designer_embarrassed
- Clippy's comeback as a Microsoft 365 emoji, GeekWire (2021): https://www.geekwire.com/2021/clippys-comeback-microsoft-tweet-promises-return-software-assistant-office-365-emoji/
- Clippy rises from the dead in major Copilot update, The Register (2025): https://www.theregister.com/2025/10/24/microsoft_clippy_copilot_update/

# Windows 95 Launch: The $300 Million Night of 1995

URL: https://404memoryfound.com/posts/the-night-windows-95-launched.html
Author: Theo Lindqvist (404 Memory Found)
Published: 2026-04-05  Updated: 2026-09-20
Topics: Software & Apps, Then vs Now

**Summary:** Microsoft released Windows 95 on August 24, 1995 behind a marketing campaign reported at $300 million, and stores opened at midnight to sell a $209.95 box of software. It moved about 1 million copies in four days and 40 million in its first year. Windows 95 is no longer a supported product: Microsoft ended support on December 31, 2001, and the only way to run it in 2026 is emulation.

**Key facts:**
- Launched: August 24, 1995, by Microsoft
- Launch price: $209.95 retail, $109.95 upgrade (1995)
- Status today: Unsupported since December 31, 2001; runs only in emulators
- Owner today: Microsoft, which still owns the code
- Replaced by: Windows 98 (June 1998), then Windows XP (October 2001)

## What did Windows 95 actually change about using a PC?

Before August 1995, a PC running Windows 3.1 dropped you into Program Manager, a grid of boxes inside boxes, with MS-DOS underneath it. Opening a program often meant knowing a path and typing it. There was no single obvious place to start.

Windows 95 added one. The Start button sat in the bottom left corner, and a taskbar ran along the bottom showing every open program by name. A minimized window no longer vanished. Right-clicking finally did something useful almost everywhere.

Long file names arrived with it. The old eight-character limit turned a school paper into ENGESS~1.DOC; Windows 95 let it be English Essay Final Draft.doc. Windows Explorer replaced File Manager, and a My Computer icon on the desktop put the hard drive, the floppy drive and the CD-ROM drive in one window.

Underneath, Windows 95 moved consumer PCs to a largely 32-bit design while keeping 16-bit code for compatibility, and it introduced Plug and Play, which was meant to detect new hardware instead of making owners set IRQ numbers by hand. The first version of DirectX shipped in the same period and set Windows up as the PC gaming platform it still is.

## Why did Microsoft spend $300 million on an operating system?

To make a piece of software the news rather than a product release. The Windows 95 campaign was reported at $300 million, and Goldman Sachs analyst Rick Sherlund told The Spokesman-Review on launch day, "I think this is unprecedented in breadth and scope."

The money bought stunts that had nothing to do with computing. The Empire State Building in New York was lit in the colors of the Windows logo. In Toronto, a 328-foot Windows 95 banner hung from the CN Tower. In Britain, Microsoft paid for 1.5 million copies of The Times to be handed out free, roughly twice the paper's daily circulation at the time.

It also bought music and television faces. Microsoft licensed the Rolling Stones' 1981 single "Start Me Up" for the advertising; press reports in 1995 put the fee at between $8 million and $14 million, and lower figures have circulated since. Microsoft then commissioned a 30-minute tape, the Microsoft Windows 95 Video Guide, starring Jennifer Aniston and Matthew Perry of Friends, and billed it as the first "cyber sitcom." It sits on the Internet Archive now and it has aged badly.

None of this was normal for software in 1995. Apple would not saturate popular culture on that scale until its portable music campaigns the following decade.

## What happened on launch night, August 24, 1995?

Stores opened at midnight. CompUSA (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-compusa-still-around.html) and other chains ran launch-night events, and people queued outside to buy a boxed operating system with a suggested retail price of $209.95, or $109.95 as an upgrade from Windows 3.1, according to The Seattle Times in June 1995. Street prices were often lower.

Microsoft's own event ran on the lawn of its Redmond campus. More than 12,500 people were invited, a crew of over 200 spent 20 days building the site, and Jay Leno co-hosted with Bill Gates. Gates got the line of the night: "Windows 95 is so easy even a talk-show host can figure it out."

The selling was real, not just the staging. UPI reported that Windows 95 moved about 1 million copies at retail in its first four days. Seven million copies went out in the first five weeks, and Microsoft said it had shipped 40 million units worldwide by the first anniversary in August 1996.

The box mattered too. Buyers got a CD-ROM or, if their PC had no CD drive, 13 floppy disks in a high-capacity format, along with a manual and a holographic certificate of authenticity. The first thing most of them heard after setup finished was the startup chime Brian Eno wrote (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/windows-95-startup-sound-brian-eno.html).

## What went wrong with Windows 95?

It crashed. The bridge between 16-bit and 32-bit code was fragile, memory management was thin, and running too many programs at once could take the whole machine down. Most applications had no autosave in 1995, so a lockup cost whatever was on screen.

Plug and Play worked often enough to matter and failed often enough to earn the nickname Plug and Pray. Sound cards, modems and printers fought over the same resources, and clearing a conflict could mean editing a configuration file or driving back to the store for different hardware.

The published requirements also understated what the system needed. Microsoft listed a 386DX processor, 4 MB of RAM and 50 to 55 MB of free disk space, then recommended a 486 with at least 8 MB. Plenty of buyers upgraded and found that their machine technically ran Windows 95 and practically could not.

Compatibility cut both ways. Some Windows 3.1 programs misbehaved, and DOS games in particular could be awkward, which is how households ended up dual-booting. That problem never fully went away, as anyone trying those titles on Windows 11 (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/run-90s-pc-games-windows-11.html) finds out.

## Can you still run Windows 95 in 2026?

Not as a supported product. Microsoft ended mainstream support for Windows 95 on December 31, 2000, and extended support on December 31, 2001, which made it obsolete under the company's lifecycle policy. It has not been sold or patched since, and Microsoft still owns the code.

What people do instead is emulate it. The Internet Archive hosts a pre-installed Windows 95 disk image that boots in a browser tab through DOSBox, and browser emulators built on the v86 engine run the same thing by translating x86 instructions into WebAssembly. Locally, 86Box, PCem and VirtualBox will all boot a Windows 95 image on current hardware. All of it is slower and buggier than the real thing was on period hardware, and none of it belongs on the open internet.

The design outlived the code. Windows 98 arrived in June 1998, Windows XP moved consumer Windows onto the NT kernel in October 2001, and Windows 8 tried to drop the Start menu in 2012. Users pushed back hard enough that Microsoft put it back in Windows 10 in 2015. The taskbar, the Start button, the clock in the corner and the recycle bin are all still roughly where Windows 95 put them.

The internet part landed as well. Windows 95 shipped without a web browser, but it carried a TCP/IP stack, and Internet Explorer arrived first in the Plus! add-on pack and later inside the operating system itself. That decision fed the antitrust case against Microsoft and the collapse of Netscape Navigator (https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-netscape-lost-the-browser-war.html).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When did Windows 95 come out?

Windows 95 went on sale on August 24, 1995, with stores across the United States opening at midnight to sell it. Microsoft launched it at an event on its Redmond campus co-hosted by Bill Gates and Jay Leno.

### How much did Windows 95 cost when it launched?

Windows 95 carried a suggested retail price of $209.95 for the full version in 1995 and $109.95 for the upgrade aimed at people already running Windows 3.1, according to The Seattle Times. Shops frequently sold both for less.

### Can you still run Windows 95 in 2026?

Only through emulation. Microsoft ended support for Windows 95 on December 31, 2001, and the operating system has not been sold or patched since. Emulators such as 86Box and pre-installed browser images on the Internet Archive will still boot Windows 95 in 2026.

- Microsoft Launches Hard Sell of Windows 95 (The Spokesman-Review, 1995): https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1995/aug/24/microsoft-launches-hard-sell-of-windows-95/
- Windows 95 sets sales record (UPI Archives, 1995): https://www.upi.com/Archives/1995/08/29/Windows-95-sets-sales-record/2741809668800/

- Windows 95 (Wikipedia): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_95
